courses.name: General Physics II
weekTopics: Nomenclature of an alternating supply: the sinusoidal waveform with its positive and negative half-cycles, the instantaneous value v = Vmax sin(wt), and the relations w = 2*pi*f = 2*pi/T linking angular frequency, frequency and period
Peak value and peak-to-peak value: the peak (maximum) value Vmax is the largest instantaneous value measured from zero, and the peak-to-peak value is 2*Vmax

RMS (effective) value defined as the steady direct current or voltage that would dissipate the same average power in the same resistance, giving Irms = Imax/sqrt(2) = 0.707*Imax and Vrms = Vmax/sqrt(2), with Vmax = sqrt(2)*Vrms = 1.414*Vrms

Why the factor 1/sqrt(2) appears: the mean of sin^2(wt) over a complete cycle is 1/2, so the mean square is Imax^2/2 and its root is Imax/sqrt(2); the mean of the sinusoid itself over a full cycle is zero, and the rectified half-cycle mean is (2/pi)*Imax = 0.637*Imax, giving form factor 1.11 and peak factor 1.414

Average power in an AC circuit: Pav = Irms^2 * R = Vrms^2/R = Vrms*Irms = (1/2)*Vmax*Imax for a resistor, with maximum instantaneous power Pmax = Vmax*Imax = 2*Pav, and generally Pav = Vrms*Irms*cos(phi) where cos(phi) = R/Z is the power factor

Phase relationships of the passive elements with a sinusoidal supply: voltage and current in phase in a resistor; voltage leading current by 90 degrees in an inductor, with reactance X_L = 2*pi*f*L; voltage lagging current by 90 degrees in a capacitor, with reactance X_C = 1/(2*pi*f*C); neither reactance dissipates average power

Series RLC circuits as second-order circuits in which the current is common to all components while the voltage drops are out of phase, so Kirchhoff's voltage law is applied vectorially: Vs = sqrt(V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2) and Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2), with I = Vs/Z

Phase angle and circuit character: tan(phi) = (X_L - X_C)/R, so X_L > X_C gives an inductive circuit with the current lagging and X_C > X_L a capacitive circuit with the current leading; at series resonance X_L = X_C, f0 = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C)), Z falls to R, the current is a maximum and the power factor is unity

courses.name: Elementary Mathematics II (Calculus)
weekTopics: Higher-order derivatives are derivatives of derivatives: f''= (f')', f'''= (f'')', and generally f^(n)(x) = d/dx[f^(n-1)(x)] with f^(0)(x) = f(x), n a non-negative integer

Notation for the orders: prime f', f'', f''' then bracketed f^(4), f^(5), ..., f^(n); Leibniz d^2y/dx^2, d^3y/dx^3, d^ny/dx^n; and the operator form D_x^n y, where the superscripts count differentiations and are not exponents
Why d^2y/dx^2 is not (dy/dx)^2 and f^(n)(x) is not [f(x)]^n: d^2y/dx^2 is the operator d/dx applied twice, (d/dx)(dy/dx), so the counter sits on the d and on the whole dx
The physical chain for displacement s(t): s' is velocity, s'' is acceleration, s''' is jerk and s^(4) is jounce, with speed increasing exactly when velocity and acceleration have the same sign
The sign of f'' as concavity: f'' > 0 means concave up with increasing gradient, f'' < 0 means concave down, and a point of inflection requires f'' to change sign, not merely to be zero

The second-derivative test at a stationary point: f'(a) = 0 with f''(a) > 0 gives a local minimum, with f''(a) < 0 a local maximum, and with f''(a) = 0 the test is inconclusive so the sign of f' either side must be used

Calculating higher-order derivatives by iterating the Week 5 rules, including the repeated product rule (uv)'' = u''v + 2u'v' + uv'', repeated chain rule where the inner derivative reappears once per order, and implicit second derivatives that require substituting dy/dx back in

General nth-derivative patterns: e^(ax) -> a^n e^(ax), sin x -> sin(x + n*pi/2), 1/x -> (-1)^n n! x^-(n+1), ln x -> (-1)^(n-1) (n-1)! x^-n, and a degree-n polynomial whose nth derivative is the constant a*n! and whose (n+1)th derivative is zero

courses.name: Introduction to Problem Solving
weekTopics: Definition: a pseudocode is a textual representation of the sequence of operations in a computer program, or the textual representation of an algorithm, written in a form that makes it easily convertible into programming statements of any language

What it is for: writing all the main steps of an algorithm in a language very similar to English, the rule of thumb that you write the pseudocode first when you are struggling to start a program, and the technique of writing the pseudocode into the file as comments and then filling in the actual code between them

The rules that govern pseudocode: each line contains only one statement, keywords are written in capital letters, statements must be language independent and not in a particular programming language, and the body of every construct is indented

The eight constructs and their skeletons: SEQUENCE (with the verbs READ/OBTAIN/GET, PRINT/DISPLAY/SHOW, COMPUTE/CALCULATE/DETERMINE, SET/INIT, INCREMENT/BUMP, DECREMENT), FOR ... ENDFOR, WHILE ... ENDWHILE, REPEAT ... UNTIL, IF-THEN-ELSE-ENDIF, CASE ... OTHERS ... ENDCASE, CALL with and RETURNING, and EXCEPTION with WHEN inside a BEGIN ... END block

Where each loop tests its condition: FOR sets all the necessary conditions at the beginning/top, WHILE sets some condition at the top and other conditions in the body so its body may run zero times, and REPEAT-UNTIL sets its condition at the ending/bottom so its body always runs at least once; FOR i = a TO b runs b - a + 1 times because both bounds are inclusive

Algorithms versus pseudocode: an algorithm is a step-by-step procedure that can be expressed in any language - natural language, programming code or mathematical symbol - and is precise and well defined, while pseudocode is a high-level, informal representation of it in a combination of natural and programming language elements, not meant to be executed as the actual code

The seven steps of writing a pseudocode - problem definition, identification of main steps, header writing (name, purpose, inputs and outputs), using variables and data structures, using constructs to describe logic, using clear and concise language, and testing and refining - applied to the course's worked problem of counting passes and failures and deciding whether tuition should be increased

Advantages (no special software needed, understandable by anyone because the language is close to English, easily modified, structured concepts easily implemented) and disadvantages (no generally accepted standards so styles vary, not visual compared with flowcharts, and slower to read and understand than a flowchart)

courses.name: General Physics Practical II
weekTopics: Aim of the experiment: investigate the charging characteristics of a capacitor and determine its capacitance and time constant

Theory of the capacitor: two conductors separated by a distance d with plate area A and a dielectric of permittivity epsilon, so C = epsilon*A/d; charge stored is Q = CV; capacitors pass AC and block DC and are used as filters in DC supplies and as energy-storage banks

Charging law: V(t) = V0 * (1 - e^(-t/tau)), where charge transfers until the p.d. between the conductors equals the p.d. across the charging device's terminals, and the current I = (V0 - V)/R falls as V rises

Time constant: tau = RC in seconds with R in ohms and C in farads; tau is the time to charge to 63.2 percent of maximum or discharge to 36.8 percent of the initial value, with about 99.3 percent reached after 5 tau, so increasing R at fixed C increases tau and the circuit charges more slowly

Apparatus and circuit: voltmeter, power supply, charging circuit (capacitor, resistor, switch key), stopwatch and wires in the Praxilabs virtual RC Circuit Charging laboratory, with the voltmeter in parallel across the capacitor

Procedure: connect the circuit, set the supply output voltage, close the switch key and record the voltmeter reading every 10 seconds until maximum voltage, taking at least 10 readings, then end the trial and download the data sheet

Data analysis and graph: plot V on the y-axis against t on the x-axis, find 63.2 percent of the maximum voltage and trace to the time axis to read tau; alternatively plot ln(V0 - V) against t for a straight line of gradient -1/tau and intercept ln V0

Calculations and errors: obtain C = tau/R and the percentage error = (theoretical - experimental)/theoretical x 100, worked for the sample trial (V0 = 1 V, R = 10 kohm, tau about 9.97 s giving C about 997 microfarads, 0.3 percent error), plus precautions and sources of error such as reaction time, voltmeter loading, dielectric leakage, component tolerance and lead resistance

courses.name: Nigerian Peoples and Culture
weekTopics: Nigeria's indigenous trade system thrived between 1500 and 1800 AD, shaped by geography and natural resources, with regions specialising in agriculture, trade or craftsmanship and exchanging what they produced for what they lacked

The Niger River was pivotal to the growth of indigenous trade, international markets drew traders from other regions, and inter-group exchange produced cultural diffusion alongside the movement of goods; the apprenticeship system passed skills and knowledge down the generations
Colonial intrusion disrupted the indigenous system, transforming Nigeria's precolonial economy into the Western capitalist economic model and altering social and political structures with it

At independence agriculture was the hub of the economy: over fifty per cent of GDP before independence and over 75% of the workforce in 1960, with Development Corporations significant in the regional political structure, and GDP growth rising from 1.89% in 1960 to 4.89% in 1965, Nigeria being tipped for the world's 20 largest economies by 1980 ahead of Malaysia

The coups and the civil war truncated economic progress, the 1970s oil boom was not saved for rainy days, agriculture was abandoned for easy oil money, and the mid-1980s crunch brought austerity measures under the Buhari regime followed by the IMF-pressured Structural Adjustment Programme

SAP further weakened the economy: the currency began a downward movement and the manufacturing base was destroyed as imported goods made local products uncompetitive on price and quality; the second oil boom of the 1990s was looted by Sani Abacha into foreign banks

The democratic era: GDP growth rose from 0.58% to 6.59% after 1999, Obasanjo secured $20 billion in debt relief and reserves above $64 billion, reserves fell to $34 billion by 2015 under Goodluck Jonathan despite oil above $100, and from 2014 US shale oil cut American purchases, India replaced the US as the major buyer, and the budget has run a deficit financed by borrowing

Causes of Nigeria's economic woes -- over-dependence on crude oil, corruption, banking insider abuse and capital-market round-tripping, poor economic policies, violence and pipeline vandalisation, and the absence of economic planning -- and the solutions proffered, from diversification and curbing corruption to electricity, industrial parks, local refining, lower cost of governance, effective tax collection and tourism

courses.name: Communication in English II
weekTopics: Three written forms defined: a summary condenses a larger text to its main ideas and essential information; a letter is a written message to a specific person or group; a report is a formal document presenting information, analysis, findings and conclusions on a specific issue

The eight ordered steps of summary writing: read carefully, identify the thesis, highlight key points, condense in your own words, maintain the original structure, eliminate unnecessary details unless crucial, check coherence, review and revise
Summary-writing conventions: own words throughout, no new material, no personal opinion, no direct quotation, roughly one third or less of the original length

The nine ordered steps of letter writing: identify purpose and audience, choose the format, greeting, introduction, body in organised paragraphs, politeness and tone, closing, closing salutation, review and edit

The five key parts of the sample letter - greeting, opening sentence, statement of purpose, closing, signature - plus the convention that 'Yours sincerely' follows a named salutation and 'Yours faithfully' an impersonal one
The eleven ordered steps of report writing, from defining the purpose and gathering data through methodology, findings, conclusions and recommendations to references, appendices and final review

The standard report sections and what belongs in each: introduction (topic, purpose, scope), methodology (how data were gathered, for transparency and reliability), findings (evidence, with graphs, charts or tables), conclusions (interpretation, no new data), recommendations (actionable steps)
Worked samples traced through: a condensed summary of a passage on politics, a letter of appreciation from Hollie Holdings, and a report on global poverty section by section

courses.name: Introduction to Web Technologies
weekTopics: HTML forms as the mechanism for collecting user input: the form element with its action, method and enctype attributes, and controls such as text fields, checkboxes, radio buttons and buttons

Accessing and manipulating form elements from JavaScript with getElementById, getElementsByTagName and getElementsByClassName, and working with the value, type and name properties (input.value is always a string)

Client-side form validation for required fields, email format and password strength, intercepting the submit event with event.preventDefault(), why server-side validation remains mandatory, and input sanitisation as a defence against XSS and CSRF

Events and event handling: the four components (event source, event type, event listener, event object), the submit / reset / change / focus events, addEventListener, and event propagation through nested elements
Asynchronous programming in JavaScript: callbacks passed as arguments, promises with .then() and .catch(), and async/await with try...catch, plus best practices for avoiding nested callbacks
The event loop and JavaScript's single-threaded concurrency model: synchronous code runs first, then queued promise microtasks, then timer callbacks such as setTimeout(fn, 0)

ES6 (ECMAScript 2015) features: block-scoped let and const, arrow functions with lexical this, template literals, destructuring, spread and rest operators, classes, modules, and transpilation with Babel
DOM manipulation and AJAX: selecting, modifying, creating and appending elements; XMLHttpRequest versus the promise-based Fetch API; JSON as the exchange format; and the same-origin policy with CORS

checks.topic:
Week 6 higher-order derivatives, exactly as the deck builds them.

That f″ is obtained by differentiating f′ again, and no new rule is introduced.

The power rule f′ = nx^(n−1), and the NOTE that the derivative of a constant is 0.

Rewriting √(x³) as x^(3/2) before differentiating.

The chain rule f′(x) = y′(u)·u′(x), and why sin(5x) keeps depositing a factor 5 while e^(3x) keeps depositing a 3 without ever changing sign.

The quotient rule [v·u′ − u·v′]/v², and why ln(1 + x²) needs it at every order after the first.

The notation f⁽⁴⁾(x) = (f‴(x))′.

questions.q: The SECOND-ORDER DERIVATIVE slide says how the second derivative is obtained. In her phrasing, it is obtained
options: by differentiating the first derivative again
by differentiating the original function with respect to a second variable
by differentiating the original function and multiplying the result by 2
questions.concept: What 'higher-order' actually instructs you to do
questions.why: Her line is exactly 'The second derivative is gotten by differentiating y′ again' — you feed the answer you already have back into the same machinery. Option 2 reads the double prime as a power; f″ and (f′)² are different functions, as x^(3/2) shows immediately. Option 3 imports partial derivatives, which the deck never mentions and which need a function of two variables. Option 4 confuses the order counter with a multiplier — nothing is multiplied by 2 anywhere in her working.

questions.q: In her sin(5x) + e^(3x) example the coefficients of the trigonometric term run 5, then 25, then 125 across the first three derivatives. Why do they keep growing?
options: Because the argument 5x is raised to a higher power at each order
Because the chain rule supplies the inner derivative 5 afresh at every differentiation
Because the notation d²y/dx² and d³y/dx³ squares and cubes the coefficient
Because sin(5x) has period 2π/5, and the period appears in the derivative
questions.concept: Why the chain factor reappears at every order
questions.why: The chain rule as she states it, f′(x) = y′(u)·u′(x), applies again every time you differentiate, and u = 5x always contributes u′ = 5 — so the coefficient is multiplied by 5 once per order: 5, 25, 125. Option 1 is false: the argument stays 5x throughout, it is the coefficient in front that changes. Option 3 treats the Leibniz superscript as an algebraic power; it is a counter. Option 4 is a true fact about the function that plays no part in differentiating it.

questions.q: For f(x) = ln(1 + x²), which rules does the deck use to reach the second derivative?
options: The quotient rule for the first derivative, then the chain rule for the second
The chain rule for the first derivative, then the quotient rule for the second
The product rule for the first derivative, then the chain rule for the second
questions.concept: The rule is chosen by the shape of what you are differentiating now
questions.why: ln(1 + x²) is a composite, so the chain rule gives f′(x) = 2x/(1 + x²). That answer is a quotient, so the second derivative needs the quotient rule — she says so explicitly: 'The first derivative is a quotient.' Option 1 swaps the order and would need a quotient to start with, which ln(1 + x²) is not. Option 2 misses that the chain rule has nothing to act on once the composite has been unwrapped. Option 4 misreads 2x/(1 + x²) — or the original — as a product.

questions.q: The FOURTH DERIVATIVE slide ends with a note on notation. It says f⁽⁴⁾(x) can also be written as
questions.concept: The bracketed superscript counts differentiations
questions.why: The fourth derivative is the derivative of the third, which is what (f‴(x))′ says; the brackets on the 4 exist precisely to stop it being read as a power. Option 1 is that misreading, and for f(x) = ln(1 + x²) the two are wildly different. Option 2 reads it as a value of f at 4 — the same confusion that produced the deck's own misprints 'f(2) = ln x' and 'f(2) = xeˣ'. Option 3 invents a constant multiple.

questions.q: Differentiating y = 3 tan x + 3 gives dy/dx = 3 sec²x. What has happened to each of the two threes?
options: The multiplying 3 stays and multiplies sec²x; the added 3 differentiates to 0
The multiplying 3 vanishes and the added 3 survives
questions.concept: Constant multiple survives, added constant dies
questions.why: A constant multiplier is pulled outside the derivative and stays — she writes 3·d(tan x)/dx — while an added constant differentiates to 0, which is the bold NOTE on the FIRST-ORDER DERIVATIVE slide, d(4)/dx = 0. She even writes the '+ 0' rather than dropping it silently. Option 2 keeps a constant that must vanish. Option 3 applies the constant rule to a multiplier, which it does not govern. Option 4 gets both backwards.

questions.q: Why does she rewrite f(x) = √(x³) as y = x^(3/2) before differentiating?
options: Because the square root of a cube is undefined for negative x
Because the power rule f′ = nx^(n−1) can only be applied to something already written as a power of x
Because the second derivative of a square root would otherwise not exist
Because fractional exponents differentiate to zero
questions.concept: Rewriting as xⁿ is what makes the power rule applicable
questions.why: The only rule she has for this function is f′ = nx^(n−1), and it needs to see an exponent n. Once √(x³) is x^(3/2), n = 3/2 and the rule runs twice without any new machinery: (3/2)x^(1/2), then (3/4)x^(−1/2). Option 1 raises a domain point that is true but irrelevant to why the rewrite is done. Option 3 is false — existence is not the issue. Option 4 confuses a fractional exponent with a constant; only constants differentiate to 0.

questions.q: A student memorises the quotient rule as [u(x)v′(x) − v(x)u′(x)]/(v(x))². What does that do to the ln(1 + x²) working?
options: Nothing, because subtraction of the two products is symmetric here
It produces the negative of the correct derivative at every order
It leaves the second derivative correct but breaks the third
questions.concept: Why v·u′ must come first in the quotient rule
questions.why: Swapping the two products negates the numerator, so f″ would come out as (2x² − 2)/(1 + 2x² + x⁴) instead of (2 − 2x²)/(1 + 2x² + x⁴) — the right expression with the wrong sign — and the error then propagates through the third and fourth orders. Option 1 is false: a − b and b − a differ whenever a ≠ b. Option 2 confuses the numerator order with the squared denominator. Option 4 wrongly suggests the mistake is self-correcting at one order.

questions.q: On her APPLICATION TO THE REAL-WORLD slide, what do the second and third derivatives of a car's position represent?
questions.concept: Physical reading of the second and third derivatives
questions.why: Her words: the second derivative 'gives us the acceleration (how the car is speeding up or slowing down)' and the third 'tells us about jerk (how the acceleration is changing)'. Option 1 is off by one order — velocity is the first derivative. Option 2 has the right two words in the wrong order, so it makes jerk-free nonsense of the third derivative. Option 3 is off by two orders, since displacement is the position function itself.

questions.q: Explain what makes a derivative 'higher-order', and why this week introduces no new differentiation rules at all.
questions.concept: Higher-order differentiation as iteration of Week 5 rules
questions.why: A good answer says: a higher-order derivative is any derivative beyond the first, obtained by differentiating the previous derivative again — f″ = (f′)′, f‴ = (f″)′, f⁽⁴⁾ = (f‴)′ — so the nth derivative is written f⁽ⁿ⁾(x). No new rule is needed because at every stage you are differentiating an ordinary function of x with the ordinary rules: power, chain, quotient, product. What changes from order to order is only which rule the current expression demands, and her SUMMARY slide puts it exactly that way — the rules are 'applied iteratively'. The ln(1 + x²) example is the demonstration: the chain rule once, then the quotient rule three times, because the shape of the expression changed after the first step.

questions.q: In her result d³y/dx³ = −125 cos(5x) + 27e^(3x), explain why the exponential term is positive while the trigonometric term carries a minus sign.
questions.concept: Sign behaviour of eᵘ versus sin and cos under repeated differentiation
questions.why: A good answer separates the two terms. For e^(3x): d(eˣ)/dx = eˣ, so the exponential reproduces itself exactly and the only thing each differentiation adds is a chain factor 3 — 3, 9, 27 — all positive, and no differentiation can ever introduce a minus. For sin(5x): the derivatives cycle sin → cos → −sin → −cos, so a sign appears at the second differentiation and is still there at the third; combined with the chain factors this gives 5 cos(5x), then −25 sin(5x), then −125 cos(5x). The answer should draw the moral: the minus belongs to the trigonometric term alone, and writing −125 cos(5x) − 27e^(3x) applies it to a term that can never be negative for real x.

questions.q: The THIRD-ORDER DERIVATIVE slide asks for 'the third derivative of f(2) = ln x'. Say what is wrong with that as printed, what she must have meant, and how you can tell.
questions.concept: Reading a misprinted question against the working that follows it
questions.why: A good answer says that f(2) is a number — the value of f at x = 2 — and a number has no derivative with respect to x, so 'the third derivative of f(2)' is meaningless as written. The intended question is: for f(x) = ln x, find f‴(2). The evidence is the slide's own last line, 'Thus, f‴(2) = 2/2³ = 2/8 = 1/4', which evaluates the third derivative at x = 2. The answer should note that the same misprint recurs on the TASK slide, 'f(2) = xeˣ', so it should be read the same way — find f‴(2) — and that flagging it matters because copying 'f(2) = ln x' into an exam script would be marked wrong even though the arithmetic that follows is right.

questions.q: Her SUMMARY slide lists the product rule among the rules used for higher-order derivatives, yet none of her six worked examples uses it. Where in the deck is it actually needed, and what does applying it there involve?
questions.concept: The one place the product rule is required, and why every order needs it again
questions.why: A good answer identifies the second TASK slide, f(x) = xeˣ, as the only place: it is a product of x and eˣ, and neither factor is constant, so (uv)′ = u′v + uv′ is unavoidable. It should then show that the rule is needed afresh at each order, because each result is still a product: f′ = 1·eˣ + x·eˣ = (x + 1)eˣ; f″ = 1·eˣ + (x + 1)eˣ = (x + 2)eˣ; f‴ = 1·eˣ + (x + 2)eˣ = (x + 3)eˣ. A strong answer adds that each differentiation simply adds 1 to the bracket, and that since the slide's 'f(2)' means evaluate at 2, the answer is 5e². It should also note the scope point: the SUMMARY lists rules the deck names, not only rules it demonstrates.

questions.why: Her wording is 'the maximum instantaneous value that a waveform reaches during one complete cycle… typically measured from the zero reference point', so the reference point is the axis. Option 2 is the trough-to-crest swing, which is twice the peak — a quantity this deck never names or uses. Option 3 is the rms value: slide 10 says AC ammeters and voltmeters are designed to read rms, so a meter never shows you the peak. Option 4 is the rectified half-cycle mean, 0.6366 I_max, which appears only as a diagram label and is never defined.

questions.q: Slide 9 opens by saying that a direct average of an alternating current 'gives no information (or useless)'. What exactly is wrong with it?
options: The average is undefined because the current changes direction
Over a complete cycle the positive and negative half-cycles cancel, so the mean is zero for every amplitude
The average depends on where in the cycle you start measuring, so it is not unique
The average is correct but too small to measure with ordinary instruments
questions.concept: Why the full-cycle mean of an alternating quantity carries no information
questions.why: The instantaneous value is positive through one half-cycle and negative through the other, and the two halves are equal in area, so the mean is exactly zero — the same zero for a 1 A supply and a 1000 A supply, which is why it carries no information. Option 1 confuses 'the mean is zero' with 'the mean does not exist'; it exists and equals 0. Option 3 is false for a whole number of cycles: the mean is zero from any starting point. Option 4 invents an instrumental problem where the problem is mathematical — a zero mean would predict zero heating, which is plainly wrong.

questions.q: She fixes the problem by squaring: I² = I²_max sin²ωt. What does the squaring achieve, and what does it cost?
options: It doubles the frequency, which makes the average easier to compute
It converts amperes to watts, so the result is already a power
It removes the sign, so the negative half-cycle no longer cancels the positive one — at the cost that the answer must be square-rooted at the end to return to amperes
It removes the time dependence entirely, leaving a constant
questions.concept: Squaring kills the sign, and the final root undoes the unit damage
questions.why: I² is never negative, so its graph (her slide-9 picture) sits wholly above the axis and has a genuine non-zero mean, I²_max/2. But I² is in A², so the square root at the end is not decoration — it is what returns the answer to amperes. Option 1 is a true side effect of squaring a sinusoid but not the reason she does it. Option 2 confuses I² with I²R; squaring a current does not by itself produce a power, since R is missing. Option 4 is false — I² still oscillates, as her diagram shows; only its average is constant.

questions.q: Slide 7 gives ω = 2πf = 2π/T. Which statement about these three quantities is correct?
options: ω and f are the same quantity written in different letters, both in hertz
T is measured in hertz and f in seconds
ω is in hertz, and multiplying by 2π converts it to radians
f is in Hz and T in s with f = 1/T, while ω is in rad s⁻¹ and is 2π times larger than f
questions.concept: Units of ω, f and T, and the factor 2π between ω and f
questions.why: f counts cycles per second (Hz), T is the seconds per cycle (s), and ω measures the angle swept per second, so ω = 2πf rad s⁻¹ because one cycle is 2π radians. At 50 Hz, ω = 314 rad s⁻¹ — the two numbers are not interchangeable, and putting f where ω belongs is out by 6.28. Option 1 collapses the distinction the slide exists to make. Option 2 swaps the units of T and f. Option 3 has the direction of the conversion right but attaches the wrong unit to ω itself.

questions.q: Slide 10 ends: 'rms values are used when discussing alternating currents and voltages because AC ammeters and voltmeters are designed to read rms values.' Taken with the slide-5 definition, what does a meter reading of 240 V on an AC supply tell you?
options: The supply would heat a given resistor at the same average rate as a steady 240 V DC supply, and its instantaneous voltage reaches about 339 V
The instantaneous voltage never exceeds 240 V, that being the largest value the supply produces
The voltage averaged over a complete cycle is 240 V
The peak voltage is 170 V, since the rms is the larger of the two figures
questions.concept: Reading an rms figure back as a statement about heating and about the peak
questions.why: The rms value is defined by equal power dissipation in a resistive load, so 240 V rms and 240 V DC heat the same resistor identically; and V_max = 1.4142 × 240 = 339 V, so the instantaneous value does exceed the meter reading for part of every half-cycle. Option 2 confuses rms with peak. Option 3 confuses rms with the full-cycle mean, which is exactly zero. Option 4 uses the factor backwards and asserts a peak smaller than the rms, which no waveform can have.

questions.q: Slide 8 writes I = V/R = (V_max/R) sin ωt = I_max sin ωt. Which pair of conclusions does that chain establish?
options: That the current lags the voltage by 90°, and that I_max = V_max/R
That the current and the voltage share the same sin ωt and so are in phase, and that I_max = V_max/R
That R changes with frequency, and that I_rms = V_max/R
That the current is constant while the voltage alternates, and that I_max = V_max R
questions.concept: What Ohm's law applied to a resistor fixes: the phase and the amplitude relation
questions.why: Dividing V_max sin ωt by the constant R leaves the same sin ωt, so nothing is shifted in time — in a resistor voltage and current rise, fall and cross zero together — and matching the result to I_max sin ωt identifies I_max = V_max/R. Option 1 imports a 90° shift that belongs to inductors and capacitors, neither of which is in this deck. Option 3 crosses an rms value with a peak value, out by √2, and makes a constant depend on frequency. Option 4 multiplies where Ohm's law divides, and would give amperes as volt-ohms.

questions.q: 'Root mean square' names three operations. In what order are they applied to the instantaneous current?
options: Take the root, then the mean, then square the result
Take the mean, then square it, then take the root
Square it, then take the mean of the squares, then take the root
Square it, then take the root, then average the result
questions.concept: Reading the name RMS backwards to get the order of operations
questions.why: The name is read from the outside in: the root of the mean of the square. Squaring first is what removes the sign; averaging second gives I²_max/2; rooting third returns the answer to amperes as 0.7071 I_max. Option 1 reverses the order completely. Option 2 averages the raw current first, which gives zero, so squaring and rooting a zero still leaves zero. Option 4 undoes the squaring before the average is taken — the root of I² is the magnitude of I, whose average is the rectified mean 0.6366 I_max, not the rms.

questions.q: Which of these does the Week 6 deck actually contain?
options: The condition for series resonance, X_L = X_C
The impedance of a series RLC circuit, Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²)
Kirchhoff's voltage law applied by vector addition of component voltages
The average power in a resistor, P_av = I²_rms R = V²_rms/R
questions.concept: The scope boundary of this deck
questions.why: P_av = I²_rms R and P_av = V²_rms/R are the two lines of slide 15, and P_av is computed in her Question 3. The other three belong to the week's separate summary sheet and to the Week 7 deck on phasor diagrams and power; reactance, impedance, phase angle and resonance appear nowhere in these 21 slides. Knowing the boundary matters: a Week 6 answer built on impedance is answering a question she has not yet asked, and it costs time that should go on the three practice questions.

questions.q: State the deck's definition of the rms value, and explain what the word 'equivalent' is doing in it.
questions.concept: RMS is defined by equal power dissipation, not by the shape of the waveform
questions.why: A good answer quotes slide 5: the rms value is a measure of the magnitude of an alternating current or voltage, representing the equivalent direct current value that would produce the same amount of power dissipation in a resistive load. On 'equivalent': it does not mean the AC and the DC are the same current — the AC is changing direction continuously and the DC is steady — it means they are interchangeable for one specific purpose, heating a resistance. So a 240 V rms supply and a 240 V DC supply make the same lamp equally bright and deliver the same average watts to the same resistor, which is exactly her slide-10 picture of an AC waveform set beside a flat 240 V DC line. The answer should draw the consequence: because the definition is about power, and power goes as the square, the rms is a root-mean-square rather than any kind of plain average.

questions.q: Reproduce her slide-9 argument in your own words: why a plain average fails and why squaring rescues it.
questions.concept: The argument from a zero mean to the mean square
questions.why: A good answer runs it as an argument in three steps. First the problem: an alternating current is positive through one half-cycle and negative through the other, and the two halves have equal area, so averaged over a complete cycle it is exactly zero — her words, 'Both alternating voltage and current have a zero value. So direct average gives no information (or useless).' Zero is the answer for every amplitude, so it distinguishes nothing, and it would falsely predict no heating. Second the fix: square the current, I² = I²_max sin²ωt. A square is never negative, so the negative half-cycle no longer cancels the positive one and the graph of I² sits wholly above the axis, oscillating between 0 and I²_max about a mean of I²_max/2. Third the correction: I² is in A², so take the square root at the end, giving I_rms = I_max/√2 = 0.7071 I_max in amperes. It is worth adding that squaring is not an arbitrary trick — power in a resistance goes as I², so the mean of I² is precisely the quantity that determines the heating.

questions.q: Slide 15 says: 'Recall that the power, P = I²R. By replacing I with I_rms, we have the average value of power.' Explain why that substitution needs no correction factor, and state the two forms she ends with.
questions.concept: Why substituting I_rms into P = I²R gives the true average power
questions.why: A good answer says that the average of a product with a constant is the constant times the average, so the average of I²R is (I²)_av times R — and (I²)_av is by definition I²_rms, since I_rms is the square root of the mean square. The substitution is therefore an identity, not an approximation, and no factor is lost or gained. It should contrast this with the current itself: substituting the average current would give zero, and substituting I_max would give twice the true power, because (I²)_av = ½I²_max. The two forms are P_av = I²_rms R and, applying Ohm's law with V_rms = I_rms R, P_av = V²_rms/R, both in watts with I in amperes, V in volts and R in ohms. A good answer may close by noting that the same reasoning is why the maximum instantaneous power is V²_max/R, exactly twice P_av.

questions.q: Her waveform diagram carries three labels: Peak Value (I_m), Average Value (I_av) = 0.6371 I_m, and RMS Value (I_rms) = 0.707 I_m. Explain what the middle one is, why it is not the rms value, and why you should not build an answer on it this week.
questions.concept: Distinguishing the rectified half-cycle mean from the rms value
questions.why: A good answer identifies the middle label as the rectified mean — the average of the waveform over a single half-cycle, taken so that the full-cycle zero is avoided — and says plainly that it is a different average from the rms: the rms squares before averaging, the rectified mean does not, so 0.7071 I_max and 0.6366 I_max are answers to different questions. It should note two further things. First, the deck never defines, derives or uses this quantity anywhere — it exists only as a label on a picture, and every calculation in the deck uses 0.7071. Second, the printed figure 0.6371 is itself slightly wrong: the rectified mean of a sinusoid is 2/π = 0.6366 I_max. So the correct exam behaviour is to know what the label means, quote 0.6366 if ever asked, and use 0.7071 for every actual calculation in this week's material.

checks.topic:
Pseudocode concepts: what a pseudocode is and what it is for.

The rules that govern it. The eight constructs, and where each one tests its condition. The seven steps of writing one.

Its stated advantages and disadvantages, and how it relates to an algorithm and to a flowchart

questions.q: Last week's deck defined a flowchart as 'a graphical representation of the sequence of operations in a computer program'. How does this week's deck define a pseudocode?
options: As a step-by-step procedure for solving a problem, which may be expressed in natural language, programming code or mathematical symbols
As a simplified programming language whose statements a compiler converts directly into a working program
As a textual representation of the sequence of operations in a computer program, or the textual representation of an algorithm
As a set of comments written into a source file to describe code that has already been written
questions.concept: the definition of a pseudocode, and the word that separates it from a flowchart
questions.why: The two definitions are the same sentence with 'textual' in place of 'graphical', which is exactly what the Pseudocodes I mid-lesson question tests ('A pseudocode is a graphical representation...' -> No). Option a is the definition of an ALGORITHM, and the giveaway is 'mathematical symbols', since pseudocode by definition uses natural and programming language elements. Option b is the 'pseudocode is nearly code' error: it is written in a form easily convertible into programming statements, which is not the same as being convertible by a compiler, and it is not meant to be executed as the actual code. Option d inverts the comments-first technique: the pseudocode becomes the comments, but it is written BEFORE the program, not as a description of code that already exists.

questions.q: A student's pseudocode contains the single line 'System.out.println(total);'. One rule is broken. Which, and why does that rule exist?
options: The one-statement-per-line rule, because printing is really two tasks - fetching total and displaying it - and each task must sit on its own line
The language-independence rule: pseudocode statements must not be written in a particular programming language, because anyone should be able to read them and convert them into any language
The capital-letters rule, because println is the output keyword on this line and keywords must be written in capitals so they stand out from other words
No rule is broken: the line holds one statement, it is understandable, and it would convert into working code without any change at all
questions.concept: language independence, and the two properties it protects
questions.why: The line is Java. Pseudocode statements are required to be language independent, not in a particular programming language, for two reasons the course states elsewhere: anyone can understand pseudocode since the language is close to English, and it is written in a form that makes it easily convertible into programming statements - any language's statements. A Java line is readable only by Java programmers and is already committed to Java, so it does neither job; 'PRINT total' or 'DISPLAY total' is the pseudocode. Option a misapplies a real rule: one statement per line means one task per line, and displaying a value is one task. Option c also misapplies a real rule: capitals are for pseudocode keywords, and println is not one - capitalising it gives SYSTEM.OUT.PRINTLN, which is still Java. Option d is the reading of the rules as style advice, when 'it converts to code without any change' is precisely the fault.

questions.q: One loop must keep reading results while a condition set at its top still holds, with further conditions inside the body deciding what happens on each pass. A second must run a number of times that is fixed entirely before it is entered. Which two constructs, in the course's own terms?
options: The first is FOR, since all its conditions are set at the beginning/top; the second is WHILE, since it runs a desired number of times
The first is REPEAT-UNTIL and the second is FOR, since only REPEAT-UNTIL is allowed to carry conditions in the body of its statements
The first is WHILE, which sets some condition at the beginning/top and other conditions in the body; the second is FOR, which sets all the necessary conditions at the beginning/top
Both are WHILE loops, because FOR is only a shorthand for a WHILE whose counter has been written out in full at the top
questions.concept: where each loop construct sets its conditions
questions.why: The course distinguishes the loops by the placement of the conditions: FOR executes statements a desired number of times based on setting ALL the necessary conditions at the beginning/top; WHILE does so based on setting SOME condition at the beginning/top and OTHER conditions in the body of the statements; REPEAT-UNTIL sets some condition at the ending/bottom and other conditions in the body. 'Some at the top, others in the body' is WHILE; 'all at the top' is FOR. Option a swaps the two, which is what a vague memory that both test at the top produces. Option b picks REPEAT-UNTIL on the strength of 'conditions in the body', which WHILE has too - the discriminator is the top/bottom placement. Option d is a true-sounding fact from programming practice that answers a different question: the course names them as separate constructs on exactly this distinction.

questions.q: In the CASE skeleton, what is OTHERS for, and what is CASE said to be?
options: OTHERS lists the variables that the expression does not test; CASE is a more generalised form of the FOR loop
OTHERS is the default sequence, run when none of the listed conditions holds; CASE is a more generalised form of the conditional statement that IF-THEN-ELSE also provides
OTHERS is the handler for values the expression cannot take; CASE is the construct out of which EXCEPTION and WHEN are built
OTHERS repeats the whole CASE for any conditions still left over; CASE is a more generalised form of REPEAT-UNTIL
questions.concept: CASE as the generalised conditional, OTHERS as its default branch
questions.why: The course introduces CASE as also using conditional statements to change the normal flow of operation of an algorithm, but represented in a more generalised form - so its neighbour is IF-THEN-ELSE, not a loop. In the skeleton, condition 1 to condition n are the alternatives and 'OTHERS: default sequence' catches everything that matched none of them, which is what stops the construct doing nothing at all. Options a and d both attach CASE to a loop, the first reading 'generalised' as 'repeated for each condition' and the second making the same error with the other loop. Option c is the near-miss worth knowing: OTHERS handles a value the expression DID take that you did not list, whereas an exception handler deals with an event that occurs while the program runs - nothing in CASE is about failure.

questions.q: In 'CALL SquareRoot with orbitHeight RETURNING norminalOrbit', what do 'with' and 'RETURNING' each name?
options: 'with' names the routine that is called, and 'RETURNING' names the routine control comes back to when it finishes
'with' names the data type of the argument supplied, and 'RETURNING' names the data type of the result produced
'with' names the class in which the object is defined, and 'RETURNING' names the object that the call creates
'with' names the argument passed into the routine, and 'RETURNING' names the variable that receives the value handed back
questions.concept: reading a CALL - arguments in, result out
questions.why: The course's four examples make the pattern plain: CALL AvgAge with studentAges (argument only), CALL Swap with CurrentItem and TargetItem (two arguments), CALL getBalance RETURNING aBalance (result only), and CALL SquareRoot with orbitHeight RETURNING norminalOrbit (both). The name straight after CALL is the routine; 'with' introduces what is passed IN; RETURNING names the variable that receives what comes OUT. Option a misreads 'with' as naming the routine, which leaves SquareRoot unexplained, and treats RETURNING as a return of CONTROL rather than of a VALUE - control always resumes at the line after the CALL, so nothing would need naming. Option b invents data-type declarations, which belong to the 'using variables and data structures' step. Option c stretches the course's remark that CALL can be used for defining class objects over the whole line.

questions.q: Both CASE and EXCEPTION/WHEN pick one set of statements out of several. What distinguishes them?
options: Nothing structural: EXCEPTION/WHEN is simply CASE written for errors, and either may be used wherever the other one is
CASE may only test numeric expressions whereas WHEN may test any expression at all, which is why exceptions were given their own keyword

CASE chooses among expected values of one expression as part of the normal flow; WHEN clauses sit in the EXCEPTION part of a BEGIN...END block and run only when an unexpected or unwanted event occurs as the program runs
CASE is evaluated once before its block runs, while WHEN is re-evaluated after every statement in the block, which is what makes exception handling the slower of the two
questions.concept: selection among expected values vs handling an unexpected event
questions.why: CASE is part of the plan: you know the expression, you list its possible values, and one branch is taken every time the construct is reached. EXCEPTION/WHEN is the opposite arrangement - the statements between BEGIN and EXCEPTION are the ones meant to run, and the WHEN clauses run only when unexpected or unwanted events take place while the program is running, which the course names as exception handling. On a run where nothing goes wrong, no WHEN clause is entered at all, which no CASE can say of itself. Option a is the tempting summary 'EXCEPTION is CASE for errors', right about the shape and wrong about the trigger. Option b invents a restriction on CASE that the skeleton 'CASE expression OF' does not carry. Option d invents an execution model and reasons about speed, a question pseudocode cannot ask, since it is not executed.

questions.q: The course lists as a disadvantage that pseudocode 'takes a longer time to read and understand' than a flowchart, even though it is written in near-English. What is the mechanism behind that?
options: Pseudocode is always longer than the flowchart of the same algorithm, because each symbol expands into several lines of text that must all be read

A flowchart shows its structure at a glance in shapes and arrows; a pseudocode reader must rebuild the control flow line by line, and must first decode the writer's own style, since no accepted standards exist
Pseudocode borrows its keywords from several programming languages at once, so a reader has to know all of those languages before following any of it
Pseudocode cannot show repetition directly, so a reader has to reconstruct every loop by hand from the statements that are being repeated
questions.concept: why a textual notation costs the reader more than a graphical one
questions.why: The course's contrast is that flowcharts are visual and easily understandable while pseudocodes are not visual, and the reading-time complaint follows from it. In a chart the control flow is drawn: a loop is an arrow you can see going back, a branch is a fork you can see splitting. In pseudocode the same structure is only implied by keywords and indentation, so the reader must simulate the flow mentally. The other stated disadvantage compounds it: since there are no generally accepted standards, anyone can write pseudocode in their own way, so the writer's conventions must be worked out before the logic can be read. Option a confuses length with difficulty and is not reliably true. Option c invents a mixed-language claim that the language-independence rule forbids. Option d is false - repetition is exactly what FOR, WHILE and REPEAT-UNTIL are for.

questions.q: Which statement about algorithms and pseudocode is correct on the course's account?
options: An algorithm may be written in any notation or language while pseudocode is written in a combination of natural and programming language elements, and the algorithm is the precise, well-defined one
Pseudocode may be written in any notation or language while an algorithm must be written in a combination of natural and programming language elements, and the pseudocode is the precise one
An algorithm is a representation of a pseudocode, produced once the pseudocode has been coded in a specific programming language and tested
An algorithm and a pseudocode are two names for one thing, since both are step-by-step procedures and neither of them is executed by a machine
questions.concept: algorithm vs pseudocode - the four contrasts the course draws
questions.why: The course states them in a row: an algorithm is a step-by-step procedure for solving a problem and can be expressed in any language - natural language, programming code or mathematical symbol; pseudocode is a high-level representation of an algorithm using a combination of natural and programming language elements, without following any specific language's syntax strictly; algorithms are usually represented as pseudocode during early software development stages, before being coded; and algorithms have precise and well-defined procedures while pseudocode is more high level and informal. Option b is the mid-lesson question's own distractor, the two terms reversed, and it also reverses the precision claim, so remembering only 'one of them is the precise one' does not rescue you. Option c reverses the direction of representation and the order of work. Option d collapses a real distinction: both are unexecuted, but the algorithm is the method and the pseudocode is one way of writing it down.

questions.q: The course recommends writing the pseudocode into a file AS COMMENTS, then filling in the actual code between those comments. Explain what problem this solves, why the course describes it as 'writing the comments for our program before writing the program', and what specifically would go wrong with the technique if the pseudocode had been written in one language's syntax.
questions.concept: pseudocode as the scaffolding of the source file
questions.why: The problem it solves is the one the course names in its rule of thumb: if you want to develop a new computer program and you are struggling with how to start the development, write a pseudocode first. The difficulty at the start is not the syntax but deciding what the steps are and in what order; writing them as comments lets you settle the whole sequence - inputs, loop, branches, outputs - while nothing in the file has to compile. Once the sequence is right, each comment is a specification for the lines beneath it, and the job shrinks from 'write a program' to a series of small local translations. Because the pseudocode was written before any code and stays in the file, we are essentially writing the comments for our program before writing the program: the commentary is not a later gloss but the design that produced the code, which is also why the comments genuinely describe what the code does. If the pseudocode had been written in one language's syntax, three things break. It stops being a design, since you have committed to that language's constructs, types and library calls before deciding whether they suit the problem. The comments become useless as comments, restating the code below them line for line instead of saying what it is for. And it fails the language-independence rule and the reason behind it: it is no longer easily convertible into the statements of ANY language, and it can no longer be read by anyone who does not know the one you chose.

questions.q: State the rules that govern the writing of a pseudocode and, for EACH one, name the specific ambiguity or failure it prevents - not what the rule says, but what a reader would be unable to work out if the rule were ignored.
questions.concept: each rule removes one ambiguity from a notation with no grammar
questions.why: ONE STATEMENT PER LINE. Pseudocode gives the computer a list of tasks to implement in a sequential manner, so the line is what carries the order. Ignore it - 'SET total TO 0; READ n; SET total TO total + n' - and the reader can no longer tell how many tasks there are, cannot cite a step by position, and cannot see whether a step was left out; worse, once several tasks share a line, indentation applies to the group rather than the task, so it stops saying which construct they belong to. KEYWORDS IN CAPITAL LETTERS. Capitals are what differentiate keywords from other words. Without them, structure cannot be told from prose: does 'if the student passed' begin an IF construct or merely describe one, and is 'set total' an instruction or a variable named settotal? Since pseudocode is deliberately close to English, the capitals are the only marker that a word is doing structural work. LANGUAGE INDEPENDENCE. Without it the pseudocode is readable only by those who know the language it leaked from, and it is no longer convertible into any language - so both properties the course claims, that anyone can understand it and that it is easily convertible into programming statements, fail at once. INDENTATION OF EACH CONSTRUCT'S BODY. This is what says how far a loop or a branch extends. Without it a reader cannot tell whether a statement after an IF belongs to the THEN part or follows the whole construct, nor whether a counter is incremented inside the loop or once after it - and the deck's own solution shows the damage, with 'add one to student counter' left outside a WHILE that therefore never advances. (The rules slide is cut off after three rules while the week's Summary sheet says four should be followed; indentation is the fourth, and every worked example in the deck obeys it.)

questions.q: List the seven steps of writing a pseudocode in order. Then explain precisely what separates PROBLEM DEFINITION from IDENTIFICATION OF MAIN STEPS, and what separates USING CONSTRUCTS TO DESCRIBE LOGIC from USING CLEAR AND CONCISE LANGUAGE, since in each pair the second step looks like more of the first.
questions.concept: the seven steps, and the two pairs that are easily collapsed
questions.why: In order: problem definition; identification of main steps; header writing; using variables and data structures; using constructs to describe logic; using clear and concise language; testing and refining. PROBLEM DEFINITION VS MAIN STEPS. Problem definition is about the problem and is written entirely in terms of inputs, process, outputs and requirements - for the tuition example, the input is the number of students and their results, the process is accepting each result and determining pass or fail, the output is the number of passes, the number of failures and the tuition decision. Nothing in it says how anything will be done or in what order; it states what a correct solution would have to take in and produce. Identification of main steps is about the SOLUTION: it breaks the problem into its integral parts and puts them in sequence - initialise the storage, set up the counters, accept a result and classify it, increment the relevant counter, display the outputs. The test that separates them: change your mind about how to solve the problem and the main steps change, while the problem definition does not. Doing the second before the first produces solutions to the wrong problem. CONSTRUCTS VS CLEAR LANGUAGE. The constructs step decides the control structure - that a WHILE will iterate over the results and an IF-THEN-ELSE will pick which counter to increment - and it is right or wrong: choose an IF where a loop was needed and the algorithm fails. The clear-language step decides the wording inside that structure, and it is about ambiguity, not correctness: 'FOR each index of string / IF string(index) is equal to hash THEN' and 'FOR i = 0 to 20 / IF string[i] = #' describe the same logic, and the course prefers the first because the second imports one language's indexing syntax. So the fifth step can leave the algorithm wrong and the sixth can only leave it unclear - but unclear is enough to fail the requirement that the constructs describe the steps without ambiguity.

questions.q: The course claims that pseudocode needs no special software, that anyone can understand it, and that it is easily modified; and it complains that there are no generally accepted standards, and that pseudocode is not visual. Explain which of the advantages and which of the disadvantages are two sides of one single property, name that property, and say what this implies about when you would choose a flowchart over pseudocode.
questions.concept: the advantages and disadvantages follow from two properties: no fixed notation, and no picture
questions.why: PROPERTY ONE: IT HAS NO FIXED SYNTAX. From this come the advantages that no special software is needed - it can be written with any text editor - that it can easily be modified, and that anyone can understand it, since the words are near-English rather than a defined grammar; and from the very same fact comes the disadvantage that since there are no generally accepted standards for writing pseudocodes, anyone can write pseudocode in their own way, leading to various styles and possible complications, especially if the pseudocode is not well written. These are one property seen from two sides: the freedom that lets you write anything is the freedom that stops a reader relying on anything. It is also why the course states rules at all - they are a voluntary standard imposed on a notation that has none, which is why breaking them costs more here than in a real language, where a compiler would object. PROPERTY TWO: IT IS TEXT, NOT A PICTURE. From this comes the rest: compared to flowcharts, which are visual and easily understandable, pseudocodes are not visual, and it takes a longer time to read and understand them - while the same property is what makes them easy to edit, since inserting a line shifts the rest down by itself, where inserting a box into a flowchart may force a redraw. IMPLICATION. Use a flowchart when the audience must grasp the shape of the logic quickly, when the structure is branching or looping enough that seeing it matters, or when non-programmers have to follow it. Use pseudocode when the design will change repeatedly, when it must be handed to programmers to convert into a specific language, or when it is to live inside the source file as its comments - and then follow the rules strictly, because they are the only standard it has.

checks.topic:
Problems-only session on Week 6 higher-order derivatives.

Compute repeated derivatives of her own functions, and one order beyond them: x⁴ + 2x³ − 15x + 4, 3 tan x + 3, √(x³) = x^(3/2), ln x, and sin(5x) + e^(3x).

Then the deck's four-order quotient-rule chain on ln(1 + x²).

Plus both TASKs she leaves unanswered: the second derivative of cos(3x), and the third derivative of xeˣ at x = 2.

And the arithmetic slip in her printed fourth derivative.

questions.q: For f(x) = x⁴ + 2x³ − 15x + 4, find f″(x).
questions.concept: Applying the power rule twice, including to the term −15x
questions.why: f′(x) = 4x³ + 6x² − 15, and differentiating again: 4x³ → 12x², 6x² → 12x, and the constant −15 → 0. Option 2 keeps the −15, forgetting that after the first differentiation it has become a constant and must die at the second — the very point of her NOTE d(4)/dx = 0. Option 3 is only the first derivative. Option 4 differentiates 6x² as 6x, dropping the factor 2 that the power supplies.

questions.q: The first TASK slide asks for the second derivative of y = cos(3x). What is it?
questions.concept: Two differentiations of a composite cosine, sign and chain factor together
questions.why: y′ = −3 sin(3x): cos differentiates to −sin and the chain rule supplies 3. Then y″ = −3·3 cos(3x) = −9 cos(3x): sin differentiates to +cos, so no second sign appears, and the chain supplies another 3. Option 1 stops after one differentiation. Option 3 loses the minus introduced at the first step. Option 4 has the right coefficient but leaves the function as sin, as though differentiating sin returned sin.

questions.q: She takes f(x) = √(x³) as far as y″ = (3/4)x^(−1/2). Continue one order: y‴ =
questions.concept: Differentiating a negative fractional power
questions.why: The power rule on (3/4)x^(−1/2) multiplies by the exponent −1/2 and drops it by one: (3/4)(−1/2)x^(−1/2 − 1) = −(3/8)x^(−3/2). Option 1 gets the coefficient but loses the minus that the negative exponent supplies. Option 2 multiplies correctly but leaves the exponent at −1/2 instead of reducing it. Option 4 reduces the exponent but forgets to multiply by −1/2 at all, so both the sign and the magnitude are wrong.

questions.q: For y = ln x she reaches y‴ = 2x⁻³. What is y⁽⁴⁾?
questions.concept: Continuing the ln x derivative chain past the third order
questions.why: Differentiating 2x⁻³ multiplies by the exponent −3 and lowers it by one: 2(−3)x⁻⁴ = −6x⁻⁴. Option 1 has the right magnitude but loses the minus that the negative exponent produces. Option 2 keeps only the sign change and forgets to multiply by 3. Option 3 uses the exponent's magnitude as the new coefficient while dropping both the existing 2 and the sign.

questions.q: She gives d³y/dx³ = −125 cos(5x) + 27e^(3x) for y = sin(5x) + e^(3x). Find d⁴y/dx⁴.
questions.concept: One more order on each term, tracking chain factors and signs separately
questions.why: d/dx[−125 cos(5x)] = −125·(−sin(5x))·5 = +625 sin(5x): cos gives −sin, and the two minus signs cancel. d/dx[27e^(3x)] = 27·3e^(3x) = 81e^(3x). Option 2 keeps the minus that has just been cancelled. Option 3 forgets the chain factor 3 on the exponential and leaves 27. Option 4 forgets the chain factor 5 on the trigonometric term and leaves 125.

questions.q: Using her f″(x) = (2 − 2x²)/(1 + 2x² + x⁴) for f(x) = ln(1 + x²), evaluate f″(2).
questions.concept: Substituting into her second derivative, denominator and sign included
questions.why: Numerator: 2 − 2(2²) = 2 − 8 = −6. Denominator: 1 + 2(4) + 2⁴ = 1 + 8 + 16 = 25. So f″(2) = −6/25. Option 1 comes from the reversed quotient-rule numerator (2x² − 2), which gives +6. Option 3 uses 1 + x² = 5 as the denominator, forgetting she squared it into 1 + 2x² + x⁴. Option 4 comes from never subtracting u·v′, leaving the numerator as 2 + 2x² = 10.

questions.q: Which of these is her third derivative of ln(1 + x²)?
questions.concept: The third order of the quotient-rule chain, numerator and squared denominator
questions.why: With u = 2 − 2x² and v = 1 + 2x² + x⁴, the numerator collects to 4x⁵ − 8x³ − 12x and the denominator is v² = 1 + 4x² + 6x⁴ + 4x⁶ + x⁸. Option 1 forgets to square the denominator. Option 2 reverses the numerator order to u·v′ − v·u′, negating everything. Option 4 mis-collects the x³ terms as −8 − 8 − 8 instead of −8 − 8 + 8, which is exactly the slip the sign of the last product invites.

questions.q: The second TASK slide asks for the third derivative of f(x) = xeˣ, evaluated at x = 2. What is it?
questions.concept: Repeated product rule on xeˣ, then substitution
questions.why: f′ = (x + 1)eˣ, f″ = (x + 2)eˣ, f‴ = (x + 3)eˣ, so f‴(2) = 5e² ≈ 36.95. Option 1 evaluates f″(2), one order short. Option 2 evaluates f′(2), two orders short. Option 3 comes from differentiating only the eˣ factor and leaving xeˣ unchanged, which ignores the product rule entirely.

questions.q: Work the first TASK slide in full: find the second derivative of y = cos(3x), naming what supplies each factor and each sign.
questions.concept: Full solution to the cos(3x) task with every factor accounted for
questions.why: A good answer takes it one order at a time. First: cos differentiates to −sin, and the chain rule f′(x) = y′(u)·u′(x) with u = 3x supplies u′ = 3, so y′ = −3 sin(3x). Second: sin differentiates to +cos, contributing no new sign, and the chain supplies another 3, so y″ = −3·3 cos(3x) = −9 cos(3x). It should say explicitly that the single minus sign was introduced at the first step and survives, so the answer is −9 cos(3x) rather than +9 cos(3x), and that the argument stays 3x throughout — only the coefficient grows. A strong answer notes y″ = −9y, the same relationship her sin(5x) example shows with −25.

questions.q: Derive f″(x) for f(x) = ln(1 + x²) from scratch, showing the chain rule step and then the quotient rule step with u, v, u′ and v′ named, exactly as slides 10 and 11 do.
questions.concept: The deck's central derivation, first two orders
questions.why: A good answer starts with the chain rule: y = ln u with u = 1 + x², so y′(u) = 1/u and u′(x) = 2x, giving f′(x) = (1/u)·2x = 2x/(1 + x²). It then observes that this is a quotient and applies f′(x) = [v(x)u′(x) − u(x)v′(x)]/(v(x))² with u = 2x, v = 1 + x², u′ = 2, v′ = 2x: f″(x) = [(1 + x²)·2 − 2x(2x)]/(1 + x²)² = (2 + 2x² − 4x²)/[(1 + x²)(1 + x²)] = (2 − 2x²)/(1 + 2x² + x⁴). Credit naming u before v in the numerator and expanding the denominator to 1 + 2x² + x⁴, since that expansion is what she carries into the third order.

questions.q: For f(x) = ln x, produce the first three derivatives in both the fraction and the negative-power form she uses, then evaluate f‴(2).
questions.concept: The ln x chain written both ways, and evaluation at a point
questions.why: A good answer gives d(ln x)/dx = 1/x, then: y′ = 1/x or x⁻¹; y″ = −1/x² or −x⁻²; y‴ = 2/x³ or 2x⁻³. It should show where each line comes from — x⁻¹ differentiates to (−1)x⁻², and −x⁻² differentiates to −(−2)x⁻³ = +2x⁻³, so the sign flips and flips back while the coefficient runs 1, −1, 2. Finally f‴(2) = 2/2³ = 2/8 = 1/4. Credit writing both forms: the negative-power form is the one that can be differentiated again, which is exactly why she supplies it at every line.

questions.q: The FOURTH DERIVATIVE slide prints the numerator of f⁽⁴⁾(x) as −12x¹² + 40x¹⁰ + 568x⁸ + 416x⁶ + 240x⁴ + 24x² − 12. Expand her own quotient-rule line and give the correct numerator, then say what remains trustworthy on that slide.
questions.concept: Checking a printed result by redoing the expansion
questions.why: A good answer expands both products. (1 + 4x² + 6x⁴ + 4x⁶ + x⁸)(20x⁴ − 24x² − 12) = 20x¹² + 56x¹⁰ + 12x⁸ − 112x⁶ − 148x⁴ − 72x² − 12. (8x + 24x³ + 24x⁵ + 8x⁷)(4x⁵ − 8x³ − 12x) = 32x¹² + 32x¹⁰ − 192x⁸ − 448x⁶ − 352x⁴ − 96x². Subtracting gives −12x¹² + 24x¹⁰ + 204x⁸ + 336x⁶ + 204x⁴ + 24x² − 12, so the printed 40, 568, 416 and 240 should be 24, 204, 336 and 204; only the x¹², x² and constant terms are right. What remains trustworthy is everything above that line: u = 4x⁵ − 8x³ − 12x, v = 1 + 4x² + 6x⁴ + 4x⁶ + x⁸, u′ = 20x⁴ − 24x² − 12, v′ = 8x + 24x³ + 24x⁵ + 8x⁷ and the quotient-rule expression are all correct — the failure is confined to the arithmetic of the expansion. A strong answer adds the check that the denominator is (1 + x²)⁴, so the correct numerator factors as −12(1 + x²)⁴(x⁴ − 6x² + 1) and f⁽⁴⁾(x) reduces to −12(x⁴ − 6x² + 1)/(1 + x²)⁴.

checks.topic:
Problems-only session on Week 6.

Convert between peak and rms in both directions, using V_rms = 0.7071 V_max and V_max = V_rms/0.7071 = 1.4142 V_rms.

Read I_max, ω, f and T straight off an equation of the form i = I_max sin ωt.

Apply Ohm's law consistently within one kind of value: I_rms = V_rms/R.

Compute power with P_av = I²_rms R = V²_rms/R and P_max = V²_max/R = 2P_av.

Includes all three of the lecturer's own practice questions with their arithmetic, the 120 V versus 250 V discrepancy between her Question 2 slides, and one wrong worked solution to diagnose.

questions.q: In SOLUTION TO QUESTION 3 (V_max = 24.0 V, f = 60.0 Hz, R = 265 Ω), what is the maximum power dissipated in the resistor?
questions.concept: Maximum power uses V_max, average power uses V_rms
questions.why: P_max = V²_max/R = 24²/265 = 576/265 = 2.174 W. Option 2 is the average power, V²_rms/R = 17²/265 = 1.09 W — the same formula with the rms voltage, and exactly half the answer. Option 3 doubles the maximum instead of the average, applying the factor 2 to the wrong quantity. Option 4 is the rms current in amperes wearing a watt label. Check any answer against P_max = 2P_av: 2.174 is twice 1.09, and if yours is not, one of the two used the wrong voltage.

questions.q: Solution to question 2 solves for the maximum voltage from an ac voltage of 250 V. What does she get?
questions.concept: Rearranging V_rms = 0.7071 V_max to find the peak
questions.why: V_max = V_rms/0.7071 = 250/0.7071 = 353.56 V, which is the same as multiplying by 1.4142. Option 1 multiplies by 0.7071 instead of dividing, 250 × 0.7071 = 176.8 V — the factor used in the wrong direction, and it gives a peak smaller than the rms, which is impossible. Option 3 changes nothing. Option 4 doubles, confusing the peak with the trough-to-crest swing. Note that her question slide sets this problem with 120 V, not 250 V; with 120 V the answer would be 169.7 ≈ 170 V.

questions.q: An alternating voltage is v = 170 sin(377t) V. What are its rms value and its frequency?
questions.concept: Reading V_max and ω off v = V_max sin ωt, then converting each
questions.why: Matching to V = V_max sin ωt gives V_max = 170 V and ω = 377 rad s⁻¹, so V_rms = 0.7071 × 170 = 120 V and f = ω/2π = 377/6.283 = 60 Hz. Option 1 quotes ω as if it were the frequency — 377 is in rad s⁻¹, not Hz, and is 2π times too large. Option 2 multiplies 170 by 1.4142 instead of by 0.7071, making the rms larger than the peak. Option 4 reads the amplitude straight off as the rms value and never converts at all.

questions.q: An alternating current of peak value 3.0 A flows through a 20 Ω resistor. The average power dissipated is
questions.concept: Putting I_rms, not I_max, into P = I²R
questions.why: I_rms = 0.7071 × 3.0 = 2.121 A, so P_av = I²_rms R = (2.121)² × 20 = 4.5 × 20 = 90 W. Equivalently ½I²_max R = ½(9)(20) = 90 W. Option 1 uses the peak current, I²_max R = 9 × 20 = 180 W, which is the maximum instantaneous power, twice the average. Option 2 applies 0.7071 a second time before squaring. Option 3 forgets the square altogether, computing I_max R = 3 × 20 = 60, which is a voltage in volts, not a power.

questions.q: A 4.0 Ω resistor is connected to an AC supply whose rms voltage is 12 V. The rms current and the average power are
questions.concept: Ohm's law used with rms values on both sides
questions.why: I_rms = V_rms/R = 12/4.0 = 3.0 A, and P_av = I²_rms R = 9 × 4.0 = 36 W, which agrees with V²_rms/R = 144/4.0 = 36 W. Option 2 converts the 12 V a second time, as if it were a peak value. Option 3 converts it in the wrong direction, multiplying by 1.4142. Option 4 has the current right but computes I R instead of I²R, dropping the square that makes it a power.

questions.q: A student answers part (b) of Question 3 by writing I = 24/265 = 0.0906 A. What has gone wrong, and what is the right answer?
options: Nothing has gone wrong; 0.0906 A is the rms current
The peak voltage was divided by R, which gives I_max, not I_rms; the rms current is 0.0642 A
The resistance should have been squared; the rms current is 0.000342 A
The 0.7071 factor must be applied twice; the rms current is 0.0454 A
questions.concept: Never cross a peak value with an rms value in Ohm's law
questions.why: 24 V is V_max, so 24/265 = 0.0906 A is I_max. Her part (a) converts first, V_rms = 0.7071 × 24 = 17.0 V, and then I_rms = 17/265 = 0.0642 A. The student's number is not wrong as a peak current — it is simply an answer to a different question, and 0.7071 × 0.0906 = 0.0642 confirms the two are consistent. Option 3 invents a squared resistance that has no place in Ohm's law. Option 4 is the opposite error, converting an already-converted figure and halving the true answer.

questions.q: An AC source has a period of 0.02 s. Its frequency and angular frequency are
questions.concept: Moving between T, f and ω with the right units on each
questions.why: f = 1/T = 1/0.02 = 50 Hz, and ω = 2π/T = 2πf = 2π(50) = 314 rad s⁻¹. Option 1 quotes the period itself as the frequency. Option 2 sets ω equal to f, the single commonest slip, out by a factor of 6.28. Option 4 swaps the two numbers and their units — 314 is an angular frequency in rad s⁻¹ and can never be a count of cycles per second here.

questions.q: A resistor on an AC supply dissipates an average power of 60 W. The maximum instantaneous power delivered to it is
questions.concept: P_max = 2 P_av in a resistor, because power goes as the square of the voltage
questions.why: P_av = V²_rms/R and P_max = V²_max/R with the same R, so the ratio is (V_max/V_rms)² = (√2)² = 2, giving 120 W. Her Question 3 shows it numerically: 2.174 W against 1.09 W. Option 1 halves instead of doubling. Options 2 and 3 apply √2 once — multiplying or dividing by 1.4142 — forgetting that power depends on the voltage squared, so the factor gets squared too.

questions.q: Work PRACTICE question 1 and PRACTICE question 2 in full, as the solution slides do. For Question 2, give the answer for both of the voltages the deck prints.
questions.concept: Rearranging the rms formula, and handling the deck's own inconsistent data
questions.why: Question 1: a household circuit at an rms voltage of 120 V. From V_rms = (1/√2)V_max, rearrange to V_max = V_rms √2, so V_max = 120√2 = 169.7 ≈ 170 V. Question 2: an ac current of 10 A and an ac voltage that the question slide gives as 120 V and the solution slide gives as 250 V. Current, unaffected by the discrepancy: I_rms = 0.7071 I_max, so I_max = I_rms/0.7071 = 10/0.7071 = 14.14 A. Voltage, both ways: with 250 V, V_max = 250/0.7071 = 353.56 V, which is what the solution slide prints; with 120 V, V_max = 120/0.7071 = 169.7 ≈ 170 V, the same answer as Question 1. A good answer names the inconsistency explicitly rather than silently choosing one figure, states the formula before substituting, and carries the unit V or A on every line.

questions.q: Work PRACTICE QUESTION 3 in full — maximum voltage 24.0 V, frequency 60.0 Hz, R = 265 Ω — showing the arithmetic for all four parts, then check your answers to (c) and (d) against each other and say which given was never used.
questions.concept: The complete resistive AC calculation, with an internal check and a redundant given
questions.why: (a) V_rms = 0.7071 V_max = 0.7071 × 24 = 16.97 ≈ 17.0 V. (b) I_rms = V_rms/R = 17/265 = 0.06415 ≈ 0.0642 A, that is 64.2 mA. (c) P_av = V²_rms/R = 17²/265 = 289/265 = 1.0906 ≈ 1.09 W; the second route on slide 15 agrees, I²_rms R = (0.0642)² × 265 = 0.004122 × 265 = 1.09 W. (d) P_max = V²_max/R = 24²/265 = 576/265 = 2.1736 ≈ 2.174 W. Check: P_max/P_av = 2.174/1.09 = 1.995, which is 2 to within the rounding of 16.97 to 17.0, exactly as required since the ratio is (V_max/V_rms)² = 2. The unused given is the frequency, 60.0 Hz: the load is a pure resistor, R does not depend on frequency, and no formula in any of the four parts contains f. A good answer states that explicitly rather than quietly ignoring it.

questions.q: An alternating current i = 8 sin(100πt) A flows through a 15 Ω resistor. Find I_max, ω, f, T, I_rms, the average power and the maximum instantaneous power, with units throughout.
questions.concept: Extracting every quantity from an equation in the form i = I_max sin ωt
questions.why: Match i = I_max sin ωt: I_max = 8 A and ω = 100π = 314.16 rad s⁻¹. Then f = ω/2π = 314.16/6.2832 = 50 Hz and T = 1/f = 0.02 s (equivalently T = 2π/ω). I_rms = 0.7071 I_max = 0.7071 × 8 = 5.66 A. Average power P_av = I²_rms R = (5.657)² × 15 = 32 × 15 = 480 W — note (I²)_av = ½I²_max = ½(64) = 32 A², so the 32 can be written down without rounding. Maximum instantaneous power P_max = I²_max R = 64 × 15 = 960 W, which is 2 × 480 W as it must be. A good answer keeps ω in rad s⁻¹ and f in Hz and does not interchange them, and notes that the angle 100πt is in radians.

questions.q: An AC voltmeter across a resistor reads 110 V and an AC ammeter in series with it reads 2.5 A. Find the peak voltage, the peak current, the resistance, the average power and the maximum power. Say why the meter readings can be used directly in Ohm's law.
questions.concept: Working backwards from meter readings, which are rms by design
questions.why: Slide 10: AC ammeters and voltmeters are designed to read rms values, so V_rms = 110 V and I_rms = 2.5 A. Peaks: V_max = 110/0.7071 = 155.6 V and I_max = 2.5/0.7071 = 3.54 A. Resistance: R = V_rms/I_rms = 110/2.5 = 44 Ω — legitimate because both readings are the same kind of value, so the 0.7071 divides out; the same R follows from V_max/I_max = 155.6/3.54 = 44 Ω, which is a useful check. Average power: P_av = I²_rms R = (2.5)² × 44 = 6.25 × 44 = 275 W, agreeing with V²_rms/R = 12100/44 = 275 W. Maximum power: P_max = V²_max/R = (155.6)²/44 = 24211/44 = 550 W, which is 2 × 275 W. A good answer states the reason the readings are rms rather than assuming it, and never mixes a peak with an rms inside one application of Ohm's law.

checks.topic:
Applied pseudocode.

Tracing a fragment line by line to what it prints. Finding the bug in a fragment and naming the rule or condition it breaks. Choosing the fragment that implements a stated task.

And the off-by-one and loop-condition traps in FOR, WHILE and REPEAT-UNTIL

questions.q:
Trace this fragment. What is printed?
SET total TO 0
SET i TO 1
WHILE i <= 4
    SET total TO total + i
    SET i TO i + 1
ENDWHILE
PRINT total
questions.concept: tracing a pre-tested counting loop, and the inclusive <= bound
