questions.why: i = 1: total = 1, i = 2. i = 2: total = 3, i = 3. i = 3: total = 6, i = 4. i = 4: total = 10, i = 5. Now 5 <= 4 is false, so the loop ends and 10 is printed, the sum 1 + 2 + 3 + 4. Option a (6) is the off-by-one from reading 'i <= 4' as 'i < 4', which drops the last pass and always loses exactly the largest term. Option c (15) comes from letting the pass with i = 5 run, that is, from testing after the body instead of before it. Option d (5) is the final value of i, printed by a student who traced correctly and then read the wrong variable - i and total end the loop holding very different things.

questions.q:
Trace this fragment. Exactly what appears on the screen?
SET n TO 10
REPEAT
    PRINT n
    SET n TO n - 3
UNTIL n < 0
options: Nothing at all, because n < 0 is false when the loop is reached
questions.concept: a post-tested loop prints before it tests, and UNTIL stops when its condition becomes true
questions.why: Pass 1 prints 10, then n = 7; 7 < 0 is false, so round again. Pass 2 prints 7, n = 4. Pass 3 prints 4, n = 1. Pass 4 prints 1, n = -2; now -2 < 0 is true and the loop stops. Four lines. Option b adds -2, which assumes another PRINT before the final test - but the decrement is the LAST statement of the body, so the value that finally satisfies the condition is never printed. Option c prints after decrementing, reading the two body lines in the wrong order. Option d is the important one: it reads UNTIL n < 0 as though it were WHILE n < 0 and, finding the condition false at the start, concludes the body is skipped. Both halves are wrong - REPEAT-UNTIL tests at the ending/bottom, so the body always runs at least once, and it stops when the condition turns true rather than running while it is true.

questions.q: Which fragment reads the marks of five students, counts how many scored 50 OR MORE, and prints that count?
options: SET count TO 0; FOR i = 1 TO 5 { READ mark; IF mark > 50 THEN SET count TO count + 1 ENDIF } ENDFOR; PRINT count
FOR i = 1 TO 5 { SET count TO 0; READ mark; IF mark >= 50 THEN SET count TO count + 1 ENDIF } ENDFOR; PRINT count
SET count TO 0; READ mark; FOR i = 1 TO 5 { IF mark >= 50 THEN SET count TO count + 1 ENDIF } ENDFOR; PRINT count
SET count TO 0; FOR i = 1 TO 5 { READ mark; IF mark >= 50 THEN SET count TO count + 1 ENDIF } ENDFOR; PRINT count
questions.concept: where the accumulator is initialised, where the read happens, and which comparison '50 or more' names
questions.why: Option d initialises count once before the loop, reads a fresh mark on each of the five passes, tests mark >= 50, and prints after the loop. Each of the others breaks exactly one of those. Option a tests mark > 50, so a student scoring exactly 50 is not counted - '50 or more' is >=, and the boundary value is the only input that separates the two fragments, which is why it is the one to test on. Option b moves SET count TO 0 INSIDE the loop, so the counter is wiped at the start of every pass and the printed value can only be 0 or 1; the plausible-looking output is what makes this bug survive. Option c reads a single mark before the loop and never reads again, so the same mark is tested five times and the answer is either 0 or 5.

questions.q:
Trace this fragment. What is printed?
SET s TO 0
FOR k = 2 TO 8
    SET s TO s + k
ENDFOR
PRINT s
questions.concept: FOR bounds are inclusive at both ends
questions.why: k takes the values 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 - that is 8 - 2 + 1 = 7 passes - and 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 + 8 = 35. Option a (27) is the sum 2 to 7, from treating the upper bound as exclusive, as a for loop in C or Java would with <. Option b (33) is the sum 3 to 8, from treating the lower bound as the value BEFORE the first pass, so the loop is imagined to increment before its first use of k. Option d (44) is the sum 2 to 9, one pass too many. Only one of the four sums can come from a correct reading of FOR k = 2 TO 8, and the check is that the answer must be 7 terms wide.

questions.q: The week's problem states that the tuition fee is increased IF MORE THAN SEVEN students pass. The course's own solution ends with the lines 'if seven or more students passed' / 'print "increase tuition"'. What, if anything, is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong: 'seven or more students passed' and 'more than seven students pass' pick out exactly the same cases
The condition is one student too generous - it raises the fee when exactly seven passed, which the problem excludes; it should test that passes is greater than seven
The condition should count failures rather than passes, since a decision about raising fees depends on how many students did not pass
The condition should compare passes with the number of students rather than with a fixed number, since seven means nothing without the class size
questions.concept: an off-by-one in a boundary condition - fragment and specification disagree on exactly one case
questions.why: 'More than seven passed' is passes > 7, first satisfied at eight. 'Seven or more passed' is passes >= 7, first satisfied at seven. They agree on every other value and differ on exactly one case, so the fault is invisible on any test data except a class in which precisely seven students pass - which is why the deck's own seventh step, testing and refining, must be done on boundary values rather than convenient ones. Option a treats the two English phrases as the same; they differ by one case. Option c redirects the test to failures, which is not equivalent - failures says nothing about passes unless the class size is known, and the requirement is stated in passes. Option d is a real design thought but not the fault: it changes the specification instead of implementing it, and the specification says seven.

questions.q:
This fragment is faulty. What exactly is wrong with it?
SET count TO 1
SET total TO 0
WHILE count <= 10
    READ x
    SET total TO total + x
ENDWHILE
PRINT total
options: total is never given a starting value, so the first addition has nothing to add to
The READ x belongs before the loop, so that the WHILE has a value of x to test on its first pass
The construct should have been REPEAT-UNTIL, because a loop that must read at least one value cannot be written as a WHILE
Nothing inside the loop ever changes count, so count <= 10 stays true, the loop never ends and PRINT is never reached
questions.concept: a loop whose condition is never affected by its body
questions.why: count is set to 1 before the loop and nothing between WHILE and ENDWHILE alters it, so count <= 10 is true on every test, the loop repeats for ever and PRINT total is unreachable; the missing line is SET count TO count + 1 as the last statement of the body. The general rule is that the body of a loop must change something the condition tests, or the loop cannot end - the same fault as last week's flowchart whose back-arrow was always taken. Option a is false: SET total TO 0 is the second line, and this distractor catches students hunting for the other bug they have been taught to look for. Option b describes a genuine pattern, the read-ahead a WHILE needs when it tests the value being read, but this loop's condition tests count, not x. Option c states a real difference between the constructs and draws a false conclusion: a WHILE can read values perfectly well, and swapping to REPEAT-UNTIL would leave the counter just as unchanged.

questions.q:
A mark of 85 is entered. What does this fragment print, and is every branch of it usable?
READ mark
IF mark >= 50 THEN
    PRINT "Pass"
ELSE
    IF mark >= 70 THEN
        PRINT "Distinction"
    ELSE
        PRINT "Fail"
    ENDIF
ENDIF
options: "Distinction", and every branch of the fragment is reachable for some mark
"Fail", because the ELSE is taken whenever a more specific test appears further down the fragment
"Pass", and "Distinction" can never be printed for any mark, since anything of 70 or more is already 50 or more
"Pass" and then "Distinction", because after the first PRINT the flow carries on into the inner IF
questions.concept: ordering nested conditions - a broader test placed first makes the narrower one unreachable
questions.why: With mark = 85 the first test mark >= 50 is true, so 'Pass' is printed and the whole ELSE part, which contains the entire inner IF, is skipped. This is not special to 85: the inner IF is reached only when mark >= 50 is FALSE, that is when mark < 50, and no such mark can satisfy mark >= 70, so 'Distinction' is dead code for every possible input. The fix is to order the tests from the most restrictive downwards - 70 first, then 50, then Fail. Option a reasons about what the author meant rather than tracing what is written. Option b treats ELSE as chosen by looking ahead at the remaining tests, when ELSE is taken only when its own IF's condition is false. Option d has the flow continuing into the ELSE part after the THEN part, which would make every IF-THEN-ELSE run both sequences - exactly one runs, which is what THEN and ELSE mean.

questions.q:
Which WHILE loop does exactly what this REPEAT-UNTIL does, for any sequence of numbers the user types?
SET t TO 0
REPEAT
    READ n
    SET t TO t + n
UNTIL n = 0
PRINT t
options: SET t TO 0; WHILE n <> 0 { READ n; SET t TO t + n } ENDWHILE; PRINT t
SET t TO 0; READ n; WHILE n <> 0 { SET t TO t + n; READ n } ENDWHILE; PRINT t
SET t TO 0; READ n; WHILE n = 0 { SET t TO t + n; READ n } ENDWHILE; PRINT t
SET t TO 0; READ n; WHILE n <> 0 { READ n; SET t TO t + n } ENDWHILE; PRINT t
questions.concept: converting a post-tested loop to a pre-tested one - negate the condition and duplicate the read
questions.why: Two changes are needed together. UNTIL n = 0 stops when the condition is TRUE, so the WHILE that keeps going must test the negation, n <> 0. And WHILE tests before the first pass, so it needs a value to test: the READ must appear once before the loop and again as the LAST statement of the body, so every value read is tested before being used. On the input 5, 8, 3, 0 the REPEAT version accumulates 5, 13, 16, then reads 0, adds it harmlessly and stops, printing 16; option b reads 5, adds it, reads 8, adds it, reads 3, adds it, reads 0 and the test ends the loop, printing 16. Option a drops the read-ahead, so the WHILE tests an n that has never been given a value - the commonest form of the mistake, and invisible in languages that quietly default a variable to zero, where the loop would simply never run. Option c forgets the negation and writes WHILE n = 0, stopping on the first non-zero value: the direct translation of 'until' as 'while'. Option d keeps the read-ahead but puts the body's READ first, so the value read before the loop is overwritten and never added; the total silently loses the first number and the fragment still prints a plausible answer.

questions.q:
Trace this fragment on the inputs 4, 7, 10, -1, showing the value of every variable after each pass, and give what is printed.
SET sum TO 0
SET count TO 0
READ x
WHILE x <> -1
    SET sum TO sum + x
    SET count TO count + 1
    READ x
ENDWHILE
SET avg TO sum / count
PRINT avg
Then say what happens if the very first value typed is -1, explain why, and give the smallest change that fixes it. Finally, explain why -1 is not included in sum even though it is read.
questions.concept: sentinel-controlled input, and the guard a division by a counter always needs
questions.why: TRACE. sum = 0, count = 0. READ x gives x = 4; 4 <> -1 is true. Pass 1: sum = 4, count = 1, read x = 7. Pass 2: sum = 11, count = 2, read x = 10. Pass 3: sum = 21, count = 3, read x = -1. The test -1 <> -1 is FALSE, so the loop ends with sum = 21 and count = 3; avg = 21/3 = 7, and 7 is printed. FIRST VALUE -1. The test fails immediately, the body never runs, and sum and count both keep their initial 0. The next line computes 0/0 - a division by zero, which has no value; a real program crashes or errors here and on paper the pseudocode simply describes nothing. Note where the fault is: the loop is correct, and only the line AFTER it is wrong, because that line assumes the loop ran at least once. SMALLEST FIX: guard the division rather than change the loop - IF count > 0 THEN SET avg TO sum / count; PRINT avg ELSE PRINT 'no data' ENDIF. Changing the WHILE to a REPEAT-UNTIL would be the wrong fix, since forcing one pass would count the sentinel as data. WHY -1 IS NOT IN THE SUM. The order of the three body statements is the whole answer: the value that reaches SET sum TO sum + x is always the one read on the PREVIOUS trip - by the READ before the loop for the first pass, and by the READ at the foot of the body afterwards. The sentinel is read by that last READ, and control then goes to the test, which leaves the loop before any statement uses it. This is the standard read-ahead arrangement, and it is why the read appears twice: it lets every value be tested before it is used, which is exactly what a sentinel requires.

questions.q:
Here is the course's own solution, as printed in the deck:
Initialise passes to zero / Initialise failures to zero / initialise student to one / WHILE student counter is active / input the next exam result / IF the student passed THEN / add one to passes / ELSE / add one to failures / add one to student counter / print the number of passes / print the number of failures / if seven or more students passed / print "increase tuition". Name FOUR faults in it - one of logic, and three of the rules and constructs the week requires - saying for each what a reader or a programmer converting it would get wrong. Then rewrite it correctly.
questions.concept: reading a pseudocode as written rather than as intended
questions.why: (i) LOGIC - AN OFF-BY-ONE IN THE THRESHOLD. 'if seven or more students passed' raises the fee when exactly seven have passed, but the problem says the fee rises only if MORE THAN seven pass. A programmer converting it writes passes >= 7 and produces software that overcharges a class in which exactly seven passed; it should be passes > 7. (ii) THE COUNTER IS INCREMENTED OUTSIDE THE LOOP. 'add one to student counter' is written flush with the unindented lines, so by the indentation it runs after the WHILE, not inside it. Read literally, nothing in the body changes the student counter, so 'WHILE student counter is active' can never turn false and the loop never ends. (iii) NO ENDIF AND NO ENDWHILE. The deck's own skeletons are IF ... THEN / sequence 1 / ELSE / sequence 2 / ENDIF and WHILE condition / sequence / ENDWHILE. Without the closers nothing marks where the ELSE branch stops and where the loop body stops, so a reader cannot tell whether 'print the number of passes' is inside the loop, printing a running total on every pass, or after it. (iv) AMBIGUOUS CONDITION AND LOWERCASE KEYWORDS. 'student counter is active' is never defined - active until what? - and the sixth step requires the constructs to describe the steps without ambiguity; the counter must be tested against something the algorithm has, namely the number of students. 'initialise', 'if' and 'print' also break the capital-keywords rule, which is what tells a reader that IF is a construct and not the English word. CORRECT VERSION: SET passes TO 0 / SET failures TO 0 / SET student TO 1 / READ number_of_students / WHILE student <= number_of_students / (indented) READ result / IF result is a pass THEN / SET passes TO passes + 1 / ELSE / SET failures TO failures + 1 / ENDIF / SET student TO student + 1 / ENDWHILE / PRINT passes / PRINT failures / IF passes > 7 THEN / PRINT 'increase tuition' / ENDIF - with the header the course requires above it (name, description, inputs, outputs). Checked on ten students with results P F P P P F P P P P: the loop runs for student = 1 to 10 and ends when student becomes 11; passes = 8, failures = 2, and 8 + 2 = 10 confirms every result was counted exactly once; 8 > 7, so 'increase tuition' is printed, whereas with one pass fewer 7 > 7 is false and nothing is printed - the case the deck's version gets wrong.

questions.q: Take this loop and the REPEAT-UNTIL written to do the same job. LEFT: SET i TO 5 / WHILE i < 5 / PRINT i / SET i TO i + 1 / ENDWHILE. RIGHT: SET i TO 5 / REPEAT / PRINT i / SET i TO i + 1 / UNTIL i >= 5. State exactly what each one prints, and explain the mechanism that makes them differ. Then change one line so that the two become identical in output, and state the general rule for when swapping WHILE for REPEAT-UNTIL is safe. Finally, say which construct you would choose for 'keep asking for the PIN until the right one is typed' and why.
questions.concept: pre-test versus post-test - the difference shows only on the pass that would not have happened
questions.why: WHAT EACH PRINTS. The WHILE prints NOTHING: i is 5 before the loop, 5 < 5 is false, and the test comes first, so the body is never entered. The REPEAT-UNTIL prints 5: the body runs before any test, printing 5 and setting i to 6, and only then tests 6 >= 5, which is true, so it stops. MECHANISM. WHILE puts the condition at the beginning/top, so the number of passes may be ZERO; REPEAT-UNTIL puts it at the ending/bottom, so the number of passes is AT LEAST ONE. The two also read their conditions in opposite senses - WHILE continues while its condition is true, REPEAT-UNTIL stops when its condition becomes true - which is why the pair carries i < 5 and i >= 5 rather than the same expression twice. MAKING THEM IDENTICAL. Change the first line of both to SET i TO 1. The WHILE then prints 1, 2, 3, 4 and the REPEAT prints 1, 2, 3, 4, and no input can separate them. GENERAL RULE: swapping WHILE for REPEAT-UNTIL is safe exactly when the loop's condition is guaranteed to permit the first pass before the loop is reached - that is, when the WHILE's condition is known to be true on entry. If it can be false on entry, the REPEAT-UNTIL executes the body once when the WHILE would not, and any read, print, increment or division in that body happens once too often. THE PIN: use REPEAT-UNTIL - REPEAT / DISPLAY 'Enter PIN' / READ pin / UNTIL pin = correct_pin. The prompt must be issued at least once, since there is nothing to test before a PIN has been typed, and REPEAT-UNTIL is the construct that guarantees exactly that; written as a WHILE it needs a read-ahead before the loop, so the prompt and the read appear twice.

questions.q:
This fragment was written to print the FIRST TEN MULTIPLES OF 3.
SET k TO 3
WHILE k < 30
    PRINT k
    SET k TO k + 3
ENDWHILE
Say exactly what it prints and how many values that is, explain where the missing one goes, and give TWO different corrections - one that changes the condition, one that uses a FOR loop instead. Then state the rule for counting the passes of FOR i = a TO b, and use it to say how many times FOR i = 3 TO 30 would run.
questions.concept: a strict inequality as the boundary of a counting loop, and the b - a + 1 rule
questions.why: WHAT IT PRINTS: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27 - NINE values. Trace the end: after printing 27, k becomes 30 and 30 < 30 is false, so the loop stops before printing 30. The tenth multiple of 3 is 30 itself, and it is lost to the strict < : the condition excludes the value that ought to have been the last one printed. CORRECTION 1 - CHANGE THE CONDITION to WHILE k <= 30, which lets the pass with k = 30 run and gives 3, 6, ..., 30, ten values. (WHILE k < 31 would work too, but it hides the boundary behind an arbitrary number, and the sixth step asks for clear, unambiguous writing.) CORRECTION 2 - COUNT THE MULTIPLES INSTEAD OF THE VALUE: FOR i = 1 TO 10 { PRINT 3 * i } ENDFOR. This is the better fragment when the count is what the specification states, because the 10 in the code is the 10 in the requirement and no arithmetic connects the two, so the off-by-one is impossible to write; it also shows the week's choice - FOR when the number of passes is known before entry, WHILE when it is not. THE COUNTING RULE: FOR i = a TO b runs the body b - a + 1 times, because both bounds are inclusive. So FOR i = 3 TO 30 runs 30 - 3 + 1 = 28 times, not 27 and not 30. The check that catches the error every time is to try the rule on a one-pass loop: FOR i = 3 TO 3 must run once, and 3 - 3 + 1 = 1.

checks.topic: The indigenous trade system of 1500 to 1800 AD and Nigeria's economic story from 1960 to the loss of the American market.

questions.q: Which river was pivotal to the growth of the indigenous trade system?
questions.concept: The Niger as the main artery of indigenous trade
questions.why: The lesson names the Niger River as pivotal: it carried bulk goods cheaply and linked the interior to the coast. The others are Nigerian rivers but are not the artery the material names.

questions.q: How were craft and trading skills transmitted in the indigenous system?
questions.concept: The apprenticeship system as skill transmission
questions.why: A young person served a master for a fixed term and was then established in the trade, reproducing the craft economy without formal schooling. Development corporations belong to the regional politics of the 1950s and 1960s.

questions.q: What share of the workforce did agriculture absorb in 1960?
questions.concept: Over 75 per cent of the workforce, 1960
questions.why: Agriculture took over 75 per cent of the workforce in 1960. The over-fifty-per-cent figure is the neighbouring trap: that is agriculture's share of GDP before independence, which is output rather than employment.

questions.q: Under which regime were austerity measures adopted after the mid-1980s oil crunch?
questions.concept: Austerity under Buhari came before SAP
questions.why: Austerity measures came first, under Buhari, as Nigeria's own response to the crunch; the Structural Adjustment Programme followed under IMF pressure. Abacha is remembered for looting the 1990s boom.

questions.q: Which country replaced the United States as the major buyer of Nigeria's crude?
questions.concept: India replaced the US as the major crude buyer
questions.why: The US, the largest buyer, announced reduced purchases in 2014 because of its own shale oil, and India replaced it. China, Brazil and Indonesia appear in the lesson only in the list of countries more populated than Nigeria.

checks.topic: Forms in JavaScript, events, promises and async/await, the event loop, ES6 and AJAX.

questions.concept: input.value is always a string
questions.why: `input.value` hands back a string even for `type="number"`, so `+` concatenates and gives '51'. Getting 6 assumes the browser converts it to a number for you, which it never does.

questions.q: Your submit handler shows an error message, then the page reloads and the message disappears. What is missing?
questions.concept: preventDefault stops the default submission
questions.why: Without `preventDefault` the browser carries out its default action and submits, reloading the page over your message. `stopPropagation` only blocks the event reaching ancestor elements, and the default still happens.

questions.q:
Why does this log `undefined`?
```js
fetch('/api/user').then(data => console.log(data.name));
```
options: The request failed, and fetch rejects on any error
The first `.then` receives a Response, not the parsed body
questions.concept: Fetch gives a Response before the body is parsed
questions.why: The first `.then` receives the Response object, and the body still has to be parsed by `.json()`, which returns another promise. Blaming a failed request is wrong too, since fetch does not reject on 404 or 500.

options: A only, until the fetch finishes
questions.concept: await pauses only its own async function
questions.why: `await` suspends just the enclosing async function, so `load` yields after A, the caller's B runs, and C follows when the promise settles. Expecting A, C, B assumes await blocks the whole page, which it never does.

options: An error: functions take fixed parameters
questions.concept: Rest gathers arguments into an array
questions.why: In a parameter list the three dots are rest, collecting every argument into one array, so `length` is 3. The identical syntax in a call or a literal would be spread, which expands a collection instead.

questions.concept: Object destructuring by key
questions.why: Destructuring pulls the value out by matching the key, so `city` holds the string 'Lagos'. It binds the value itself rather than a smaller object, which is the usual first guess.

options: An error, since classes must declare properties first
questions.concept: Class constructors assign properties on new
questions.why: `new` runs the constructor, which assigns the argument to `this.name`, so `d.name` is 'Rex'. Class syntax is a wrapper over prototypes, and properties are created by the constructor rather than declared up front.

options: An `appendChild` call to put it in the document
questions.concept: createElement builds a node; appendChild inserts it
questions.why: `createElement` only builds the node in memory, and it shows up once it is appended to an element already in the page. Styling or naming it changes nothing while it still has no parent.

questions.q: In `el.addEventListener('click', e => console.log(e.target))`, what is `e`?
options: The event object, with information about the event
The event source, the element that was clicked
The event listener that was registered
The event type as a string
questions.concept: The four components of an event
questions.why: `e` is the event object handed to the listener, and `e.target` reads the source out of it. The source is the element itself, the listener is the arrow function, and the type is the string 'click'.

questions.q: Which event fires when the user picks a different option in a `<select>`?
questions.concept: The form events named in the lecture
questions.why: `change` fires when a control's value changes, which is what picking a new option does. `focus` fires only when the control is entered, while `submit` and `reset` belong to the form as a whole.

questions.q: A comment list gains new comments while the page itself stays put. What is happening?
options: The browser reloads the page from cache each time
A CSS media query is redrawing the list
AJAX: data is fetched and the DOM updated without a reload
The form is resubmitting itself with GET on a timer
questions.concept: AJAX updates the DOM without a full refresh
questions.why: AJAX loads data in the background and updates the DOM with it, so no full page refresh is needed. A reload, cached or not, would replace the entire document, which is the thing AJAX exists to avoid.

questions.q: Which handles a rejected `await fetch(...)` inside an async function?
options: A `.catch()` on the async function's declaration
questions.concept: Error handling with async/await
questions.why: With async/await, a rejection from an awaited promise is caught by a `try...catch` wrapped around it. Checking `response.ok` matters too, but it inspects a response that has already arrived, so it cannot run first.

checks.topic: The ordered steps and conventions for writing a summary, a letter and a report.

questions.q: In summary writing, which step follows identifying the thesis?
questions.concept: Order of the eight summary-writing steps
questions.why: The order runs read carefully, identify the thesis, highlight key points, condense, maintain structure, eliminate details, check coherence, review. The other three options are all later steps in that same list.

questions.q: What must a summary be written in?
options: Your own words, with no new material or opinion
The original's own sentences, kept intact
Your own words, with your judgement of the argument
questions.concept: Summary conventions: own words, nothing added
questions.why: A summary restates the key points in your own words and carries no new material, no personal opinion and no direct quotation. Stitching the original's own sentences together fails the condensing step however short the result is.

questions.q: Which closing goes with a named recipient such as Dear Mr Azeez?
questions.concept: Yours sincerely for a named recipient
questions.why: Yours sincerely pairs with a named salutation, and the sample letter closes that way. Yours faithfully belongs with the impersonal Dear Sir or Madam.

questions.q: Which report section states the methods used to gather the data?
questions.concept: Methodology as the section on data-gathering methods
questions.why: Methodology presents the methods used, ensuring transparency and reliability. The introduction gives topic, purpose and scope, findings give the evidence, and conclusions interpret it.

questions.q: What step do summary, letter and report writing all end with?
questions.concept: The shared final step of all three procedures
questions.why: All three end with a review and revise or review and edit for clarity, coherence and accuracy that also checks the piece achieves its purpose. References and recommendations belong only to reports, and the closing salutation only to letters.

checks.topic: Charging a capacitor: the time constant, obtaining C from the graph, the circuit wiring, capacitor behaviour and the procedure.

questions.q: At one time constant, what percentage of the maximum voltage has the capacitor reached?
questions.concept: 63.2 per cent charged at t equals one time constant
questions.why: Charging reaches 63.2 per cent of maximum in one time constant; 36.8 per cent is what remains while discharging. 86.5 per cent is two time constants and 99.3 per cent is five.

questions.q: With the experimental time constant read off the graph, how is the capacitance found?
questions.concept: C = τ/R follows from τ = RC
questions.why: Since τ = RC, dividing the experimental τ by the known R gives C. Remember to put R in ohms, not kilohms, or the answer is out by a factor of a thousand.

questions.q: How is the voltmeter connected in the charging circuit?
options: In series with the switch key
questions.concept: Voltmeter in parallel across the capacitor
questions.why: The voltmeter must read the potential difference across the capacitor, so it goes in parallel with it, which is why it is made of very high resistance. Resistor, capacitor, switch and supply are the parts in series.

questions.q: What does a capacitor do to alternating and direct current?
questions.concept: Capacitors pass AC and block DC
questions.why: This is why capacitors are used as filters in DC supplies. The reverse statement is the common slip.

questions.q: How often is the voltmeter read during the trial?
options: Once at the start and once at the end
Every 10 seconds, for at least 10 readings
questions.concept: The 10-second reading interval and the minimum of 10 readings
questions.why: Readings are taken every 10 seconds until the voltage reaches its maximum, with at least ten points so the asymptote V0 is well established. That interval works because the time constant here is about 10 seconds, comfortably longer than reaction time.

recapCandidates.topic: Why impedance and AC voltages add in quadrature, not arithmetically - and why V_L or V_C can exceed the supply voltage
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: This is the topic that most reliably survives self-checking, because the wrong method produces a number that looks entirely respectable. A student who writes Z = R + X_L + X_C, or Vs = V_R + V_L + V_C, gets ohms and volts of a plausible size, with no division by zero, no negative root and no absurd magnitude to sound an alarm - so nothing in the answer itself reveals the error, and the student walks away believing the method works. Underneath it sit three separate confusions. First, students carry over the DC habit that 'in series, things add', without noticing that in DC the drops add because they all peak at the same instant, which is exactly the condition that fails here: V_R peaks with the current, V_L a quarter-cycle earlier and V_C a quarter-cycle later. Second, they treat reactance as a variety of resistance because it is quoted in ohms and does limit the current - which then makes it inexplicable why X_L and X_C should subtract from one another rather than add, since both of them 'oppose' the current. The resolution is that they oppose it a quarter-cycle apart and in opposite senses, so they are 180 degrees from each other and cancel. Third, and most tellingly, many students conclude that Kirchhoff's voltage law simply fails in AC circuits, because they can measure V_C = 160 V across a capacitor fed by a 100 V supply and see no way to reconcile it. KVL never fails: it holds instant by instant, and what is illegitimate is adding the amplitudes of quantities that never reach their maxima together. The belief survives because both the arithmetic and the vector method give the same answer in the one case students meet first - a purely resistive circuit, or one at resonance - so the error is invisible in precisely the examples used to introduce the topic.
whyQuestions: Why is the voltage across a resistor in phase with the current through it, while the voltage across an inductor is not?
Why can you not simply add V_R, V_L and V_C to get the supply voltage, when Kirchhoff's voltage law says the drops around a loop must add up to it?
Why do X_L and X_C subtract from one another in the impedance formula rather than add, when both of them oppose the current and both are measured in ohms?
Why can the voltage measured across a capacitor be several times larger than the voltage of the source driving it, without any energy being created?
Why does a series RLC circuit draw the most real power exactly at the frequency where its two reactances cancel, given that neither reactance ever dissipated any power in the first place?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
States the rule and its condition: quantities may be added arithmetically only if they reach their maxima at the same instant, which in a series RLC circuit only V_R does - so Vs = sqrt(V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2) and Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2), with tan(phi) = (X_L - X_C)/R.
Explains the mechanism, not just the formula: with the common current as reference, V_L leads it by 90 degrees and V_C lags it by 90 degrees, so V_L and V_C are 180 degrees apart and directly oppose each other, which is why they subtract; V_R is at right angles to both, which is why the resultant is a Pythagorean sum rather than a straight one.
Resolves the apparent paradox explicitly: KVL holds at every instant, so V_C larger than the supply is legal because when v_C is at its peak, v_L is at its opposite peak and v_R is passing through zero - the arithmetic sum corresponds to no instant that ever occurs - and reactances store and return energy rather than dissipating it, so the only power is I^2 R, maximised where Z is least, at resonance.
recapCandidates.workedExample:
A series RLC circuit: R = 30 ohm, X_L = 40 ohm, X_C = 80 ohm, supply 100 V rms.

Step 1 - the wrong method, so the difference is visible. Arithmetic addition would give Z = 30 + 40 + 80 = 150 ohm and I = 100/150 = 0.67 A. Nothing about that answer looks wrong.

Step 2 - the net reactance. X = X_L - X_C = 40 - 80 = -40 ohm. It is negative, so the circuit is capacitive.

Step 3 - impedance in quadrature. Z = sqrt(R^2 + X^2) = sqrt(30^2 + 40^2) = sqrt(900 + 1600) = sqrt(2500) = 50 ohm - a third of the wrong answer.

Step 4 - the current, common to all three components. I = Vs/Z = 100/50 = 2.00 A.

Step 5 - the component voltages. V_R = I R = (2.00)(30) = 60 V; V_L = I X_L = (2.00)(40) = 80 V; V_C = I X_C = (2.00)(80) = 160 V.
Their arithmetic sum is 60 + 80 + 160 = 300 V - three times the supply, and describing an instant that never occurs.

Step 6 - the vector sum, which is what KVL actually requires. V_L - V_C = 80 - 160 = -80 V, so Vs = sqrt(V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2) = sqrt(60^2 + 80^2) = sqrt(3600 + 6400) = sqrt(10000) = 100 V. Exactly the supply.
Note V_C = 160 V across the capacitor while the source is only 100 V. This is real and measurable, and it is legal: at the instant v_C reaches +160 V, v_L is at -160 V and v_R is passing through zero, so the sum at that instant is 0 V - and a quarter-cycle later v_R carries its full 60 V while the reactive pair sum to 40 V. At every instant the three add to the supply.

Step 7 - phase angle. tan(phi) = X/R = -40/30 = -1.333, so phi = -53.1 degrees: the current LEADS the supply voltage by 53.1 degrees, as a capacitive circuit must. Power factor cos(phi) = R/Z = 30/50 = 0.600 leading.

Step 8 - power, by two routes. P = Vs I cos(phi) = (100)(2.00)(0.600) = 120 W. Check: P = I^2 R = (2.00)^2(30) = 120 W. The two agree, and all 120 W is in the resistor; the inductor and the capacitor together dissipate nothing at all, merely passing energy back and forth (each of them handles I^2 X = 160 var and 320 var, which are volt-amperes reactive, not watts).

Step 9 - the resonance check. Raise the frequency until X_L = X_C. The net reactance vanishes, Z drops to R = 30 ohm - its smallest possible value - the current rises to 100/30 = 3.33 A, phi becomes 0, the power factor becomes 1, and the power rises to (3.33)^2(30) = 333 W. Nothing was 'unblocked': the cancellation of two oppositions that were already 180 degrees apart is what let the current through.

recapCandidates.topic: Loop conditions - where the test sits, and which values it lets through
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Every student can recite that WHILE tests at the top and REPEAT-UNTIL tests at the bottom, and almost none of them can use it, because the difference is invisible on the data they check their work with. A loop that is meant to run five times runs five times under either construct; the two versions separate only on the pass that would not have happened - the empty case, where a WHILE runs zero times and a REPEAT-UNTIL runs once anyway - and nobody traces the empty case unless taught to. The same blindness covers the boundary of the condition itself. A student who writes WHILE k < 30 when they meant k <= 30 loses exactly one value out of ten, and the output still looks like a list of multiples of three, so it passes the eye test that a syntactically broken fragment would fail. Underneath sit four specific beliefs. First, that UNTIL and WHILE are the same word: the student writes UNTIL count = 5 and reads it as 'keep going while count = 5', when UNTIL stops on true and WHILE continues on true, so the correct correspondence is UNTIL c = WHILE NOT c. Second, that the condition is a description of the loop's purpose rather than a test evaluated at one exact moment; a student who believes 'i <= 4' means 'four times' cannot answer what happens when i starts at 5, and cannot see that the same condition on a post-tested loop gives a different count. Third, that the body's order does not matter much - so the increment drifts out of the body, or the READ moves to the top of it, and the loop either never ends or silently drops its first value while still printing a plausible number. Fourth, that testing means running the happy path: the course's own worked solution ships an off-by-one, printing 'increase tuition' when exactly seven students pass, in a problem whose statement says more than seven, and the fault survived because seven is precisely the input nobody tries. The wrong beliefs survive self-checking because every one of them produces output of the right shape - a number, a list, a decision - and only the boundary case, the empty case and a written-out variable table can tell the right shape from the right answer.
whyQuestions: Why can the body of a WHILE loop run zero times, while the body of a REPEAT-UNTIL always runs at least once?
Why does UNTIL count = 5 correspond to WHILE count <> 5, and not to WHILE count = 5?
Why does FOR k = 2 TO 8 run seven times and not six, and why does WHILE k < 30, starting at 3 and stepping by 3, print only nine multiples of 3 instead of ten?
Why is an off-by-one in a boundary condition almost never caught by testing a fragment, and what single test would catch it every time?
Why does converting a REPEAT-UNTIL that reads data into an equivalent WHILE force the READ to be written twice, and what exactly goes wrong in each of the two ways of writing it only once?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
Names where each construct's test sits and what follows for the number of passes: FOR sets all its conditions at the beginning/top so the count is fixed before entry and equals b - a + 1 for FOR i = a TO b; WHILE sets some condition at the top, so the body runs zero or more times; REPEAT-UNTIL sets its condition at the ending/bottom, so the body runs one or more times - and states that UNTIL c is equivalent to WHILE NOT c, since UNTIL stops when its condition becomes true while WHILE continues while its condition is true.
Traces rather than describes: writes out a table of every variable after every pass, including the pass on which the loop exits, and explicitly checks the empty case (the condition false on entry) and the boundary value (the input on which >= and > disagree), because those are the only two inputs on which a wrong loop and a right loop give different answers.
States the two body rules that make a loop terminate and be correct: the body must change something the condition tests, or the loop never ends; and in a sentinel-controlled read-ahead the addition must come before the next READ, with one READ before the loop and one at the foot of the body, so that every value is tested before it is used and the sentinel is never counted as data.
recapCandidates.workedExample:
ONE TASK, THREE LOOPS, AND THE CASES THAT SEPARATE THEM.
Task: add up the first n whole numbers and print the total, for n read from the user.

(A) FOR - the count is known before entry.
READ n
SET total TO 0
FOR i = 1 TO n
    SET total TO total + i
ENDFOR
PRINT total
With n = 4: i = 1, total = 1; i = 2, total = 3; i = 3, total = 6; i = 4, total = 10. Both bounds are inclusive, so the body runs n - 1 + 1 = n times and 10 is printed.
With n = 0: the bounds 1 TO 0 give 0 - 1 + 1 = 0 passes, the body never runs, and 0 is printed. This is the case that matters.

(B) WHILE - the same thing, tested at the top.
READ n
SET total TO 0
SET i TO 1
WHILE i <= n
    SET total TO total + i
    SET i TO i + 1
ENDWHILE
PRINT total
n = 4: pass 1 total = 1, i = 2; pass 2 total = 3, i = 3; pass 3 total = 6, i = 4; pass 4 total = 10, i = 5; now 5 <= 4 is false. Prints 10 - identical to (A).
n = 0: 1 <= 0 is false at once, the body never runs, prints 0 - still identical to (A).
Note the two things that make it work: the condition uses <= (with <, the last term 4 would be lost and the answer would be 6), and the body changes i, which is what the condition tests. Delete SET i TO i + 1 and the loop never ends.

(C) REPEAT-UNTIL - the same body, tested at the bottom.
READ n
SET total TO 0
SET i TO 1
REPEAT
    SET total TO total + i
    SET i TO i + 1
UNTIL i > n
PRINT total
n = 4: total = 1, i = 2; 2 > 4 false. total = 3, i = 3; false. total = 6, i = 4; false. total = 10, i = 5; 5 > 4 true, stop. Prints 10 - identical to (A) and (B).
n = 0: the body runs anyway, total = 1, i = 2, and 2 > 0 is true, so it stops - and prints 1, not 0. WRONG.
The three loops agree on every value of n except 0, the one case where the body should not run at all, and that is the whole of the difference between a pre-tested and a post-tested loop. Note also that the condition had to be inverted: WHILE i <= n became UNTIL i > n, because UNTIL stops on true.

THE BOUNDARY, IN THE COURSE'S OWN EXAMPLE.
The problem says the fee rises if MORE THAN seven students pass; the deck writes 'if seven or more students passed'.
passes:      5      6      7      8      9
passes > 7:  no     no     no     yes    yes     <- the specification
passes >= 7: no     no     YES    yes    yes     <- the deck
They differ on exactly one input, passes = 7. Test with a class of 5, or 9, or 10 and the two versions agree, which is why the fault shipped. The rule this gives: whenever a condition contains a comparison, the test data must include the value the comparison is about, one below it and one above it.

THE READ-AHEAD, WHICH IS THE SAME PROBLEM ONE LEVEL UP.
REPEAT / READ n / SET t TO t + n / UNTIL n = 0 becomes, as a WHILE:
SET t TO 0
READ n
WHILE n <> 0
    SET t TO t + n
    READ n
ENDWHILE
PRINT t
On 5, 8, 3, 0 both print 16. Now write the READ only once and both ways fail. Put it only inside, at the top of the body (WHILE n <> 0 { READ n; SET t TO t + n }): the first test reads an n that has no value, and the first number typed is overwritten before it is added, so 5 is lost and the total is 11. Put it only before the loop: n never changes, the loop never ends. The READ appears twice because a pre-tested loop must have a value to test before its first pass and a fresh value to test before every pass after it.
